title: Mashusha rises from Amakhosi to become UK community champion
content:
Entertainment Hub
BULAWAYO-born theatre practitioner and performer Enisia Mashusha has added another accolade to an illustrious artistic career after being named Community Leader of the Year 2026 at the Goodnews Global Life Awards in the United Kingdom.
Mashusha, who is now based in the UK, received the award in August in recognition of her work in community mental wellbeing, youth empowerment and cultural wellness through her organisation, Mambokadzi Wellness.
For the veteran performer, the award is more than a personal achievement.
“Receiving the Community Leader of the Year 2026 award from the Goodnews Global Life Awards in August is a deeply humbling recognition. For me, this award is not just a personal milestone, it shows the power of community, heritage and the arts.”
Mashusha’s journey in the arts stretches back more than three decades to 1995 when she began her foundational training at the legendary Amakhosi Theatre under the late theatre icon Cont Mhlanga.
Her early years at Amakhosi laid the foundation for a career that would see her make her mark on Zimbabwe’s theatre, television, film and radio industries before taking her talents to international audiences.
In the same year she began her training, Mashusha won the Best Actress Award from the National Theatre Organisation of Zimbabwe for her performance in Hoyayaho, an Amakhosi production.
She went on to feature in several notable productions, including Stitsha, Hlengiwe Mntanami and Fragments. Her talents also extended to radio, where she starred in the drama Mopani Junction and won another Best Actress award.
Mashusha also toured extensively across Europe with Amakhosi productions, gaining international exposure and taking Zimbabwean theatre and performance to audiences beyond the country’s borders.
Her passion for dance and cultural expression later saw her establish Mambokadzi Dance Group, which she founded and continues to direct. Under her leadership, the group has earned recognition in the arts sector, including a National Arts Merit Award (NAMA) for Best Dancer of the Year.
Mashusha is using the same cultural traditions that shaped her artistic career to address a different challenge — community wellbeing.
As Founder and Executive Director of Mambokadzi Wellness in the UK, she combines Zimbabwean storytelling, rhythm, movement and theatre in community wellness programmes designed to promote mental wellbeing, inner-child healing and social connection.
“Bringing my decades of background in Zimbabwean theatre and performance into the UK community wellness space has shown me how much people need spaces to connect, express themselves and heal,” she said.
Mashusha said the award belonged not only to her but also to the people who have participated in her programmes.
“This recognition belongs to every participant, young artist and community member who has walked into a Mambokadzi space and trusted the process,” she said.
Her vision for Mambokadzi Wellness is now to expand its footprint across West Yorkshire and beyond while creating sustainable opportunities for young creatives.
A major component of the programme is youth empowerment, with Mashusha seeking to provide structured platforms for emerging artists, musicians and drummers to showcase their talents through wellness productions.
“We are building a sustainable model that uses traditional storytelling, movement and rhythm to address mental wellbeing, support inner-child healing and combat social isolation. A central part of our future is youth empowerment — providing structured platforms for emerging young artists, musicians and drummers to showcase their talents within our wellness productions.”
Mashusha is also preparing for a workshop scheduled for 18 September at Swarcliffe Community Centre in the UK, as she continues to develop programmes that bring together cultural heritage and creative health.
Her journey from the stages of Amakhosi to community wellness spaces in the UK demonstrates the versatility of the arts and the enduring power of Zimbabwean cultural expression.
For Mashusha, the mission is ultimately about using the arts to create healthier and more connected communities.
“As we move forward with upcoming events, our goal is to continue blending cultural heritage with creative health to build stronger, more resilient communities,” she said.

title: Twilight fandom helps fund Quileute Tribe’s move to higher ground
content:
This story was originally published by Underscore Native News.
Lyric Aquino
Underscore Native News + Report for America
This story is part of Underscore Native News’ reporting that explores and amplifies Indigenous climate solutions, through the Indigenous Climate Solutions Cohort. Underscore is part of a five-newsroom grant supported cohort with the Indigenous Journalists Association (IJA) and Solutions Journalism Network’s Climate Beacon Newsroom Initiative.
To many Indigenous people and Twilight Saga super fans, it’s no secret the Quileute Tribe was not compensated for the representation of its people in the popular fantasy books and subsequent films.
The Quileute people’s likeness is used throughout the franchise even as their traditional lore is misrepresented. In both the novels and movies, Quileute tribal members are portrayed as shape-shifting werewolves, often referred to as “dogs,” who are forced to cut their hair despite it being culturally significant to remain intact. The stories have been criticized for perpetuating harmful stereotypes of Indigenous people.
The tribe has found itself in an unusual spotlight: receiving global attention for a pop-culture phenomenon that amassed over $3.3 billion at the global box office without being given compensation.
“Many supporters and scholars have raised conversations about cultural representation and compensation. The Quileute Tribe did not receive royalties from the Twilight franchise despite the use of elements inspired by Quileute culture and identity,” the tribal council told Underscore Native News in an email. “Conversations about this issue have helped spark broader discussions about Indigenous representation, cultural respect, and ethical storytelling.”
Now, Twilight fans are trying to rectify the lack of financial compensation by raising funds for the Quileute Tribe’s Move to Higher Ground Project through varied creative means. From raffles, to a personal donation from the CEO of a large makeup company, to creating social media videos about the project, fans are trying to find any way they can to make a difference.
The urgent need to move
Located along the western edge of the Olympic Peninsula, the Quileute Tribe’s coastal town La Push sits at the mouth of the Quillayute River. Home to fewer than 400 people, the quaint town is just one small section of the former 800,000 acres the tribe inhabited pre-colonization.
But after signing over their land in exchange for health, education and job training as well as reserving hunting, fishing and gathering rights in their “usual and accustomed places,” the Quileute Tribe was left with a tiny parcel of land in a tsunami zone. That land has been slowly withering away due to coastal erosion, exacerbated by climate change.
“Living in a tsunami zone at the edge of the Pacific Ocean, a catastrophic earthquake can wipe out our community in less than 10 minutes — an entire generation of the Quileute people will cease to exist,” state tribal officials said on the tribe’s Move to Higher Ground Project website.
In a 2023 report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), scientists stated rising sea levels are a direct result of the planet’s rising temperatures melting snow glaciers and ice sheets, which add water to the ocean. Additionally, as water temperatures continue to warm, the volume of the ocean increases due to thermal expansion. Over time, the changing waters, intense storms and winds have led to the erosion of La Push’s shores, leaving hardly any barrier between the ocean and their land if a tsunami were to occur.
After years of lobbying the federal government for acreage, in 2012 President Barack Obama signed legislation that returned around 280 acres of Olympic National Park land to the tribe. The returned land is being used for the Quileute’s Move to Higher Ground Project, a multi-year development of an upper village located outside of flood and tsunami zones.
In 2022, phase one of the development was completed when the Quileute Tribal school was built some 250 feet above sea level. Eventually, the upper village will hold homes, an elder center, cultural facilities, tribal government offices, emergency services, parks and open spaces.
But the Move to High Ground Project is just one of many in the Pacific Northwest, including the Quinault Nation, which estimates it will cost $450 million to move its entire lower village, Taholah, a half-mile away. Similar to Quinault, the Quileute are looking for ways to continue the funding to move their citizens to safety.
“The Move to Higher Ground initiative is a multi-phase, long-term relocation effort, meaning funding needs evolve as each stage progresses,” the Quileute tribal council told Underscore. “Because development occurs in stages and depends on grants, infrastructure costs and construction timelines, the total remaining fundraising goal is ongoing rather than a single fixed number.”
The power of fandom
Twilight carries a complicated legacy when it comes to representation of Indigenous people, an issue not lost on some longtime fans like Kayla Parker. Like many preteens of the era, her obsession started in the sixth grade, when she began reading the first Twilight young adult novel.
Enraptured by the drama, edginess and whimsy of the vampire-werewolf-romance saga, she became obsessed with the franchise.
“I read the first book, bawled my eyes out, because I was like, ‘Why will a hot, rich vampire not make me immortal and give me superpowers? This is so rude. Edward Cullen should be in love with me,’” Parker said. “I was miserable.”
In 2007 she picked up the second book in the series and immediately lost interest in the plot.
“I picked up ‘New Moon’, and it’s not even about Edward, it’s about Jacob. I was sickened, I was disgusted. I was like, ‘never mind. I’m not reading this, I can’t do it.’ So then I put it aside. I did not continue reading and I did not continue watching the series.”
But in 2015 she binged the films and devoured the four books in the series, reigniting the brief obsession that had consumed her preteen brain.
But something didn’t sit right with her, particularly the parts involving the Quileute tribe. As she grew up, Parker felt uneasy about the use of the Quileute tribe’s likeness without permission and compensation. As an avid reader and consumer of the Twilight books and films, she wanted to help right the wrongdoing of the Quileute people in her own way — through social media.
Parker now serves as a moderator for a Facebook group called “Twilight Shitposting,” created in 2020 for and by fans of the book and film series to engage with each other through jokes, memes and general conversation around the topic. Six years later, the group has amassed more than 820,000 followers and is responsible for raising $117,000, according to group moderators, for the Quileute’s Move to Higher Ground Project.
Parker said the moment the group started to gain a large following she thought she could use the group’s platform to raise funds for the tribe.
“I do believe in the power of social media. I do believe in the power of collective action. I do believe in the power of reading and media, and in the things that we read and consume,” Parker said.
Starting in September 2021, the Facebook group moderators organized an online fundraiser event, encouraging members to donate at least $1 to the Move to Higher Ground Project. That first year, $6,000 was raised, with many donating more than just the dollar. Those who donated were entered into a raffle for prizes such as book covers, getting an admin to approve a post in the group, and a copy of “The Twilight Saga: The Official Illustrated Guide.”
In the years that followed, Parker said fans have offered illustrations, merchandise, art pieces and more to be part of the prize pool for future raffles.
By 2025, the annual fundraiser had gained so much popularity that the moderators gave the first 600 donors a spot on a raffle wheel to win one of 112 prizes and raised $37,000.
“I feel like, in reality, we’re doing something very small. We didn’t start anything, we didn’t originate anything,” Parker said. “We’re really just trying to shine a light on things that have already existed.”
Reflecting on fandom culture, Parker said connection from stories is inherently human.
“I think that human beings are naturally hardwired to find community and to find connection,” she said. “The power of storytelling has been as pervasive as it has been because stories are really what connect people… Twilight is what it is — it is a story.”
Parker hopes people who were associated with the Twilight franchise see the fundraiser and use it as an opportunity to make reparations to the Quileute people.
“We would love it if we could get the attention of people like Stephanie Meyer that would kind of be like, ‘Oh, you know what, maybe I should have done that. Maybe I should use my money to put it back to some people that I should have consulted with, I should have talked with,’” Parker said.
Underscore Native News reached out Stephanie Meyer, author of the Twilight Saga for comment. She did not respond to the request.
The makeup mogul
Twilight fans can choose from a vast array of licensed merchandise: socks, backpacks, bedsets, jewelry, clothing and much more. A popular trend in recent years has been makeup collaborations with brands such as ColourPop Cosmetics and Glamlite Cosmetics.
However, many fans boycott officially licensed materials because of the franchise’s history with the Quileute Tribe. When Gisselle Hernandez, CEO and founder of Glamlite Cosmetics, announced the release of her Twilight collection on Valentine’s Day in 2025, she was shocked to see so many fans talking about the Quileute Tribe and their history.
“When I started my partnership with Twilight through Paramount, I wasn’t aware that the movies and the books had been based on real people,” she told Underscore Native News.
When fans asked her if she was going to donate to the tribes, Hernandez, who had little knowledge of the Quileute people, began looking into the tribe and their Move to Higher Ground Project.
“Anything that is important to my audience is important to me,” she said. “And so I took it upon myself to begin the research.”
After learning about the history of the Quileute people and their tense history with the franchise, Hernandez reached out to the tribal council to ask for a meeting to learn more and make a personal donation. When she heard back, she immediately canceled everything she had lined up for the week and made the seven hour journey to La Push.
“I became really involved. I really wanted to be able to meet the tribe in person because I wanted to hear firsthand from them, from tribal leaders, exactly what is happening,” she said. “Why do they need these funds? And so they could share their story with the world.”
Hernandez said she was awe-struck by the beauty of La Push and the warmth of the tribe, a place and people she didn’t know were real just months prior. In her time with the Quileute Tribal Council, she took a tour with Chairman Rio Jaime and heard about the need for funds to Move to Higher Ground.
She was moved when Jaime said as a kid he used to have to do evacuation drills in case a tsunami hit. As she toured the reservation, Hernandez filmed a TikTok to help amplify the tribe’s efforts, reaching 1.3 million followers on Instagram, Tiktok and Facebook once it was posted.
“One thing about me is when I make a donation it’s never just writing a check and handing it over to people,” she said.
Hernandez also brought attention to the tribe’s rich tourism history that existed before Twilight, encouraging people to stay at the resort on Quileute lands. But after she personally donated an undisclosed five-figure sum to the tribe and released her video, Hernandez says she faced harsh backlash from the licensor of Twilight.
“By choosing to make a personal donation to the Quileute tribe, I lost certain partnerships because it was frowned upon,” she said. “Before I made the donation, I knew of the consequences and what the retaliation would be moving forward, and I still decided to do it. I believe in doing good. I believe in doing what’s right, even if it means losing opportunities and losing certain partnerships.”
Underscore Native News reached out to Paramount Pictures for comment and they did not respond to the request.
While Hernandez had plans to live out her Twilight-fantasy through releasing a makeup collection for each book, her licensing partnership quietly ended, with an announcement about the collection leaving, and after March 31, 2026, Hernandez said Glamlite Cosmetics is no longer allowed to sell anything Twilight related.
Hernandez said companies who have entered into similar licensing agreements have been offered the same choice, though she did not name those companies.
“There’s plenty of other brands that received the same restrictions and they had the same opportunity to make the donations,” she told Underscore Native News. “And instead they chose to just follow protocol, look the other way and use the story of the Quileute Tribe to make [a] profit and completely ignore an entire population of people and benefit off their name, off their story, without making that donation, just because it means it was going to be frowned upon.”
Creative fundraising to make every dollar count
In January 2026, romance author Kelsey McKnight hosted a unique fundraiser for the Move to Higher Ground Project, raising over $1,000 by raffling off a character based on the winner to be featured in the second book of her vampire romance trilogy, “Bound by Blood.” The raffle was posted on her Instagram and TikTok, as well the “Twilight Shitposting” Facebook page.
A fan of Twilight for over two decades, McKnight said her love for the franchise didn’t mean she couldn’t critique the way the Quileute people were portrayed in the books and films.
“I didn’t have the cultural knowledge that I could have or that I should have when I was younger, and I just enjoyed the books and the movies and went on with my day,” she said.
McKnight was moved by the Quileute tribe’s Move to Higher Ground effort. And, as an avid fan of the Twilight franchise, she felt like she could help right the wrongs of consuming media without a second thought by bringing funds and awareness to the initiative.
“I’m a very small fish,” she said. “If I was a big fish, like ColourPop Cosmetics, I would funnel some of that money into the group of people that [were] fetishized.”
For a little over a week, fans donated in increments of $5 per entry. McKnight hand wrote onto raffle tickets the 600 names of eager vampire-loving fans hoping to become a character in her trilogy.
After she drew a name from her Nosferatu popcorn bucket, McKnight reached out to the winner, sent her the first book, “These Immortal Vows,” and began crafting the character of the winner for her second book. With so much enthusiasm over the raffle, McKnight added a couple of small bonus winners and featured them in the second book as well.
As she begins preparations to write the third book in her trilogy, McKnight plans to do a similar raffle but on a larger scale to support the Move to Higher Ground Project.
“It happened very quickly, and it was over very quickly, but I’m hoping that at some point I can figure out a way to do something that’s a little bit bigger,” she said. “I was pleasantly surprised that there was so much interest in that particular form of fundraising. So it is something that I think would be really helpful to do for me in the future, as far as using my work to raise awareness in a creative way.”
Phases and the future
Although the legacy of the Twilight franchise is complex, Quileute tribal officials told Underscore Native News they’re thankful for fans supporting them and their movement.
“Twilight fans from around the world have shown up in meaningful ways,” the tribal council wrote in an email. “Many have turned awareness into action through donations, advocacy, and helping spread the word about the Move to Higher Ground initiative. Many fans’ donations reflect a broader desire to acknowledge Indigenous communities and support real-world needs connected to popular culture narratives.”
As an ambitious long‑term relocation effort, the project’s timeline is expected to last many years and will constantly be evolving. Development will occur in stages and depend on grants, infrastructure costs and construction timelines. Throughout the process, donations from fans will be essential for housing, community facilities and safety infrastructure.
“For all of us involved with the Move to Higher Ground initiative, the support from fans has been a powerful example of how pop culture can inspire real-world compassion and action,” the tribal council wrote. “We want everyone to know that we see you and we truly appreciate you. We see and hear your genuine desire to learn about who we are and how you can support our real life challenges.”
“Whether a donation is large or small, every single one matters,” the council continued. “What means the most to us is knowing that fans are giving what they can from the heart, and that kind of support is something we will never take for granted.”
Correction: The story previously stated the Quileute Tribe was not consulted during the creation of the Twilight Saga. Those references have been removed in response to the tribe’s clarification that filmmakers did consult them, although they did not receive compensation.

title: “La resistencia en el tiempo y el espacio de la cultura mixteca me hizo repensar el cine”
content:
Nicolás Rojas Sánchez aborda las historias de migración que le contaron los pobladores de San Juan Mixtepec, Oaxaca, quienes también actuaron en su primer largometraje
Martes 15 de septiembre de 2026, p. 7
Al filo de padecer Alzheimer, Emilia sueña con volver a ver a su hijo, quien se marchó a Estados Unidos hace 30 años. Un 24 de junio, día de San Juan, la tierra que entraña su origen y el de sus ancestros, hará posible su encuentro. La enfermedad, la vejez, la migración y la niñez son los temas que dan forma a Sókó, primer largometraje de Nicolás Rojas Sánchez (San Juan Mixtepec, Oaxaca, 1984). El cineasta cuenta con cinco cortometrajes, entre documental, ficción y experimental.
Este drama de ficción de 110 minutos, que se encuentra en etapa de posproducción desde hace dos años, fue uno de los 19 proyectos seleccionados de la octava convocatoria del Estímulo para la Creación Audiovisual en México y Centroamérica para Comunidades Indígenas y Afrodescendientes (ECAMC), organizada por el Instituto Mexicano del Cine. Está hablada en sa’an savi (mixteco), español e inglés, debido a que “la migración ha hecho que esta amalgama de culturas se fusionen”.
Aparte de dirigir la cinta, Rojas Sánchez es coguionista con Indira Velasco Viloria. Sókó es una historia inspirada en su abuela y tío. “Durante toda mi infancia escuché a mi abuela hablar de un tío que nunca conocí. Siempre esperaba el regreso de su hijo en la fiesta del pueblo; sin embargo, nunca sucedió. Con el paso de los años mi abuela empezó a confundirme con mi tío cuando comenzó a tener episodios de Alzheimer. Ésta es una historia que intenta salirse del marco, atreviéndose a otra narrativa. También en contra posición a la hipervelocidad que se vive en la actualidad”.
Rojas Sánchez estudió ciencias de la comunicación en Oaxaca, pero “la vida me especializó en el cine”. En la Ciudad de México “se me abrieron muchas puertas para entender el tipo de cintas que quería hacer”.
Comenzó su carrera en 2006 trabajando en películas con Corazón Films; primero como ayudante de arte, después hizo utilería, luego diseño de producción, asistencia de dirección y algo de actuación.
Eso “me llevó a repensar el cine desde el contexto de donde provengo, que es la cultura mixteca, con una comunidad fuerte que ha resistido al tiempo y al espacio, sobre todo en la lengua.
“La raíz siempre te llama. El hecho de regresar a vivir a Oaxaca (en 2020) implicó dejar el quehacer cinematográfico en la Ciudad de México, donde me quedaba poco tiempo para desarrollar historias propias. Este trabajo es muy demandante, especialmente en el ámbito comercial, lo que también lleva al hartazgo.
“Siempre iba y venía, aunque ahora más consciente de dejar la Ciudad de México y arrancar distinto desde Oaxaca. Ahora estamos en la Sierra Juárez colaborando con otro grupo de cineastas. Al final el cine se hace en comunidad.”
Sókó se basa en hechos reales junto con historias que se cuentan. “Insisto en que hay una investigación detrás de esto. La coguionista también es antropóloga y poeta. Al pertenecer yo a la comunidad mixteca hemos explorado por mucho tiempo. En 2024, cuando íbamos a filmar, fuimos al pueblo y estuvimos más tiempo porque allá se hizo el casting. Encontramos a personas que contaban historias como éstas. La realidad supera la ficción. Hay personas que salen y no regresan. La Ciudad de México y el mundo están llenos de personas que venimos de otros lados. Hay quienes olvidan su raíz, otras que nos gusta conectar y otras que están huyendo. En este caso la idea es reconectar toda la raíz. La cinta está basada en muchas cosas, pero es una ficción”.
Casting no tradicional
Todas las personas que actúan en Sókó son de San Juan Mixtepec, un pueblo básicamente migrante. Para esto se hizo un casting no tradicional. “Por invitación o recomendación platicamos con personas que luego se integraron, así fue como salieron niños, adultos, personas mayores, extras y músicos. Todo lo que se integra en la película es más o menos una cartografía de lo que sería mi pueblo, digamos”.
Nadie recibió una preparación actoral. “En el casting revisamos la predisposición de las personas, después las preparamos, pero no como si fuera un coach actoral porque no quería que interfiera en el lenguaje. No tenía por qué intervenir alguien que no hablara mixteco. Por ejemplo, la persona que interpreta a Emilia, cuando se hizo el casting, me sentó en una mesa y me hizo platicar toda la historia en mixteco. A partir de allí decidió hacia dónde iba su personaje.
“En otro caso, doña Gloria nos invitó a su casa, pero cuando llegamos no era sólo ella, sino 10 personas que querían hacer el casting. Aparte de platicar la historia, también hablaba de qué es el cine y cómo se hace, entender desde la intimidad como íbamos a trabajar. A partir de esto empezamos a construir los personajes. Por más que están dibujados en los guiones el trabajo con los actores siempre tiene el poder de decisión de sus personajes. El guión sólo impone el texto.
“Para mí todos son actores desde que conscientemente asumen este rol y deciden hacerlo. No se dedican a esto, por supuesto, pero es un punto y quiebre en su vida en que decidieron entregar sus vidas a ello a lo largo de los 24 días que duró el rodaje”.

title: England’s Pitt Rivers Museum announces its largest repatriation of human remains
content:
The Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford, has agreed to return a collection of human remains to the Indigenous Naga people of the Indian subcontinent. The 39 pieces of Naga remains, primarily skulls, will return to Nagaland, a small north-eastern state in India, by the end of the year.
According to The New York Times, Laura Van Broekhoven, the director of Pitt Rivers, said the handover, scheduled for November, will be the largest repatriation of human remains from the museum. She called the process a “Naga-wide movement of healing and unification”.
The Pitt Rivers Museum holds the largest collection of Naga material in the world, much of it gathered by colonial administrators in the early 20th century, a museum statement says.
In February the University of Oxford received a claim from the Forum for Naga Reconciliation, an association of 39 Naga organisations, for 40 ancestral remains kept in the Pitt Rivers Museum. The claim followed the university’s procedures for the return of cultural objects and was agreed by Oxford University Council in July. “Council agreed to the return of 39 ancestral remains, declining the return of one further remain which does not have a clear provenance as Naga,” a museum statement says.
In 2020 the museum removed all human remains from display. “Since 2020 museum officials have worked in collaboration with Naga partners, in particular the Forum for Naga Reconciliation and its Recover, Restore and Decolonise team, together with tribal Hohos, elders, churches and communities across the Naga homeland to decide how their ancestors should be cared for and returned,” the statement adds.
A delegation of 20 Naga leaders and scholars visited the Pitt Rivers Museum in June last year to see the stored remains. At the end of the visit, the Naga-Oxford Declaration on Repatriation was produced when the Naga people stated: “We are sorry that it has taken us several decades but we are here now to reclaim and return you to the homelands from where you were taken.”
According to the Pitt Rivers website, the first Naga ancestral remains were given to the institution more than a century ago by John Henry Hutton, a colonial administrator in the Indian Civil Service and an anthropologist. Most of the Naga ancestral remains now in the collection were brought to Oxford by Hutton and a second anthropologist, James Philip Mills, between 1910 and 1940.
Earlier this year, an investigation by The Guardian revealed the vast scale of human remains held in British museums and universities, prompting criticism from politicians and scholars.

title: Saket Soni Wants to Protect the Workers Rebuilding Communities After Disaster
content:
When Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans in 2005, hundreds of thousands of residents fled, many never to return. Saket Soni did the opposite: He relocated to the waterlogged city—a seemingly confounding choice to anyone who doesn’t know him. As a young community organizer, Soni had been working with renters in Chicago, many of whom were Black and from the South. “I watched Katrina unfold in their living rooms through their eyes," he says. He moved to Louisiana to support the cleanup crews. There he found a mentor in Vincent Harding, a historian and activist who'd counseled Martin Luther King Jr. "He always told me that America is a country that is still being born," says Soni. "This is a place that's still being built, and you're part of building it." Soni took it literally.
In 2017, the New Delhi emigrant cofounded Resilience Force, a nonprofit that protects the rights of workers who make a living cleaning up after natural disasters. There's a long, quiet history of disenfranchised people climbing slick ladders and crawling under wrecked, mildewing homes to make things right after devastating storms—"America’s white blood cells," as Resilience Force puts it. As extreme weather events become more severe and more frequent, this itinerant cleanup crew, often comprised of undocumented workers and likely numbering in the hundreds of thousands, is a growing sector of the economy.
TIME Trailblazers: Saket Soni
"Go to any fire- or hurricane- or flood-hit town in America, and you'll see the labor shortage," says Soni. "Even if the money comes, if the workers aren't there to repair, then people won't be coming home." Soni hopes to continue developing this much-needed workforce over the next decade.
As well as providing legal advocacy for resilience workers, Resilience Force collaborates with third-party contractors to ensure laborers get better pay and safety standards. The nonprofit also offers a structured certification program that gives workers the technical and safety skills to perform roof repairs and other hands-on, AI-proof jobs. Then it puts people on the job directly, too, a blueprint with which they've seen success in states as politically and environmentally diverse as Louisiana and Colorado. While its in-house activities are paid for by philanthropy, Resilience Force provides free assistance to uninsured homeowners when it can.
As budget and staffing cuts at the Federal Emergency Management Agency further complicate recovery for communities affected by disasters, the Resilience Force model aims to directly confront three intersecting crises: climate change, the housing shortage, and a difficult job market. Inherently, Resilience Force also addresses a fourth crisis: anti-immigration sentiment.
Soni recalls a time he arranged help for a conservative Florida family whose home had been damaged by Hurricane Michael. "There was darkness all around,” he says. “They lost their electricity. Their roof was blown. They put up a sign that said, 'Strangers will be shot.'" Nevertheless, Soni rolled up with a squad of Resilience Force workers, many of whom were immigrants, and rebuilt the house. In short order, the family took the sign down. "Everybody's focused on how polarized the country is," Soni says. "I see the opposite."

title: Tradisjonsrikt utvær legg ned: – Ei varsla krise for ærfuglen
content:
Selskapet melder sjølv om nedlegginga på Facebook, og oppgir nedgangen i ærfuglbestanden som hovudårsak.
Det markerer slutten på ein æra for ein av dei mest unike tradisjonane langs kysten vår.
I generasjonar har øyfolka på Helgeland levd i eit tett og livsviktig samspel med ærfuglen, populært kalla «ea».
Menneska har bygd reir og verna fuglane mot rovdyr i hekketida, og som takk har dei kunna sanke dei verdifulle edderduna når fuglane forlét reira utpå sommaren.
No er derimot fuglebestanden i så stor nedgang at drifta til selskapet ikkje lenger er berekraftig.
Luksusdyner til dei kongelege
– Dei siste åra har talet på ærfuglar som kjem til Lånan gått mykje ned. I år hadde vi berre halvparten så mange fuglar som i 2018, seier fuglevaktar Hildegunn Nordum.
Konsekvensen av at det blir færre fuglar på reir, er at det blir mindre edderdun og dermed færre dyner å produsere og selje.
Edderdun frå ærfugl blir rekna for å vere verdas varmaste og mest eksklusive duner. Det krevst dun frå omtrent 60 reir for å lage éi dyne av vanleg størrelse, og ei slik handlaga dyne har hatt ein prislapp på godt over 100.000 kroner.
Dynene blir rekna som ei investering som kan vare i fleire generasjonar. Blant dei som søv under desse dynene dronning Sonja. I 2007 gjekk kommunane på Helgeland saman om å gi slike dyner i 70-årsgåve til kongeparet.
Arbeidet med å reinse duna går føre seg tradisjonelt for hand på ein såkalla dunharpe for å skilje ut støv og rask, og er eit tidkrevjande arbeid.
– Det er nesten eit halvt års arbeid for å få ferdig duna til éi dyne, forklarer Nordum.
Tradisjonen med å la fuglevaktarar bygge små hus og reir til ærfuglane, for så å sanke duna når fuglane forlèt reiret, strekker seg heile 1500 år tilbake i tid.
Dette unike samspelet mellom fugl og menneske bidrog sterkt til at Vegaøyane i 2004 hamna på UNESCOs liste over natur- og kulturarven i verda.
Varsla katastrofe: – Det ser f* meg mørkt ut
Nedlegginga av Utværet Lånan AS speglar ei dramatisk utvikling som lenge har prega Helgelandskysten.
Forsking bekreftar at ærfuglbestanden i verdsarvområdet er meir enn halvert berre dei siste ti åra.
På Hysvær har fuglevaktarane Snefrid Jakobsen og Øystein Ludvigsen nyleg slått alarm om situasjonen.
– Vi reknar med cirka 80 prosent tilbakegang, kanskje meir, sidan 90-talet, seier Jakobsen om utviklinga.
Ludvigsen har uttrykt frykt for at ærfuglen på Vega kan vere heilt borte om 10–15 år viss trenden fortset.
– Det ser f*** meg mørkt ut.
Årsakene til tilbakegangen er ifølge forskinga samansette, og kjem av ein kombinasjon av klimaendringar med varmare hav, dårlegare næringsinnhald i maten deira, menneskelege forstyrringar frå båttrafikk, og dessutan auka press frå rovdyr som oter, mink, havørn og kråke.
– Kvar einaste fugl vi klarer å berge og hjelpe trygt ut i havet, er ein siger, seier Jakobsen.
– Det skjer stort sett overalt der ein har noko data. Einaste unntak, ironisk nok, ser ut til å vere indre Oslofjord. Der har det vore ein auke over dei siste åra
Det seier sjøfuglforskar Jan Bustenes i Norsk institutt for naturforsking (Nina) som nettopp har vore i felt på Vega med prosjektet «Allianse for ærfugl».
Bustenes er einige med vaktarane i at det blir ekstremt vanskeleg å få bestanden tilbake til historiske høgder.
– Spørsmålet nå er om ein i det heile klarer å berge bestanden og stabilisere han på eit nivå der han klarer å halde oppe seg sjølv, seier han.
Transportproblem gav nådestøyten
På Lånan har dei merka desse miljøendringane på nært hald gjennom dei 20 åra selskapet har eksistert.
– Det er lite mat til fuglane. Vêret har også forandra seg. Eg håpar verkeleg praten om dette kan bidra til at det blir meir forsking på kva som skjer, for det er kjempeviktig, understrekar Nordum.
Men for Lånan AS var ikkje mangelen på fugl det einaste problemet.
Den andre medverkande årsaka til avviklinga er at båtturane mellom Vega og Lånan fall bort.
Selskapet prøvde ein periode å organisere eigne turar til Lånan etter at dei faste båtturane, som i dei første åra hadde tre anløp i veka, stansa.
– Nå må vi erkjenne at vi ikkje har moglegheit for å drive dette vidare. Det lønner seg ikkje, seier Nordum.
Dette skjer sjølv om selskapet tidlegare har fått økonomiske tilskot frå blant anna Innovasjon Noreg, Nordland fylkeskommune og Riksantikvarens verdiskapingsprogram.
Sjølv om selskapet nå set punktum, vil ikkje ærfuglane på Lånan bli overlatne til seg sjølve.
– Vi skal fortsette å vere fuglevaktarar. Ea og ærfuglen er det viktigaste for oss, så den kulturarven fortset vi å ta vare på, seier Nordum.
– Men formidlingsbiten blir borte. Vi er jo det ekte, vi er jo kulturarven. Det blir borte for folk å oppleve og sjå.
Så lenge det er ærfugl og dun på øya, vil fuglevaktarane fortsette å lage så mange dyner dei kan.

title: Rwanda: How Rwanda Turned Drones Into a Development Tool
content:
When Rwanda partnered with Silicon Valley technology company Zipline to deliver blood by drones in 2016, many could have dismissed the idea as futuristic. Instead, Rwanda pioneered what was described as the world's first national-scale commercial drone delivery service designed to save lives.
Nearly a decade later, the initiative has become a powerful example of how technology can address practical development challenges.
On October 14, 2016, President Paul Kagame launched Zipline's medical delivery service in Muhanga. The mission was simple: get blood to hospitals quickly, particularly those in remote areas where distance, poor roads and difficult terrain could turn an emergency into a tragedy.
President Kagame captured the philosophy behind the initiative when he said: "Technology becomes relevant and meaningful when it works for people and addresses challenges they face daily."

That principle explains why the Rwanda-Zipline partnership matters beyond drones.
Before the service, health workers could spend hours travelling to collect blood. Today, hospitals can place orders and receive blood products within minutes. In 2023 alone, Zipline delivered 28,754 units of blood in Rwanda, with an average delivery time of 25 minutes.
The impact goes beyond speed. Research has found that drone delivery reduced in-hospital mortality from postpartum haemorrhage by 51 percent and reduced blood wastage by 67 percent.
Behind these figures are mothers who survived childbirth, patients who received urgent transfusions and doctors who could act when every minute mattered.
Dr Swaibu Gatare of the National Centre for Blood Transfusion noted that health workers saved an average of 3.1 hours per delivery, with more than 10,000 hours previously lost to road-based blood collection redirected towards patient care.
Today, Zipline delivers blood to 53 hospitals across Rwanda and operates distribution centres in Muhanga and Kayonza and soon to Karongi District. Its services have expanded to specialised medicines, children's vaccines and vaccines for domestic animals, with more than 600 essential supplies delivered daily.
Zipline co-founder and former CEO Keller Rinaudo described the challenge as a logistics problem getting essential products to people when and where they need them. Rwanda provided the environment in which that idea could be tested and scaled.
What began with blood has evolved into a broader logistics platform. Drones now support healthcare, agriculture, animal health and other essential services. In tourism, Zipline has also partnered with the Rwanda Development Board to deliver locally made products to hotels and lodges, with 20 percent of delivery fees going towards conservation in Volcanoes National Park.
The numbers demonstrate the scale. By 2025, Zipline was serving 27 of Rwanda's 30 districts and more than 900 health facilities. The company reported that its emergency deliveries had helped save more than 40,000 critical patients since 2022.
And Rwanda is not stopping there.
In February 2026, the Government signed a new expansion agreement aimed at making Rwanda the world's first country with nationwide autonomous logistics coverage and Africa's first urban drone delivery network. The expansion is expected to extend rapid drone delivery into urban areas, including Kigali.
At the 2025 Aviation Africa Summit, President Kagame said the Rwanda-Zipline partnership had been successful and that the two sides were exploring urban deliveries, emphasizing that drones "do not only save time, it also saves lives."
The evolution of this partnership demonstrates a distinctive approach to development. Rwanda did not wait for the technology to become commonplace elsewhere. It identified a problem, found an unconventional solution, created the regulatory space to test it and scaled what worked.
The lesson is bigger than Zipline.
For Africa, where geography, infrastructure and distance continue to constrain access to essential services, autonomous delivery could become part of the continent's future logistics architecture. Medicines, laboratory samples, agricultural inputs, emergency supplies and commercial goods need not always depend on congested or inadequate roads.
The real achievement of Rwanda's drone experiment is therefore not simply that machines now fly across the country's skies. It is that an idea once considered futuristic has become part of everyday life saving patients, supporting healthcare workers, delivering essential products and creating new possibilities for development.
That is what successful innovation looks like: technology becoming part of everyday life while its impact becomes impossible to ignore.
The writer is a communication specialist.

title: Desde 2025, Chiapas ha alfabetizado a 250 mil personas
content:
Viernes 11 de septiembre de 2026, p. 13
San Cristóbal de Las Casas, Chis., Galardonado con el Premio Internacional de Alfabetización Confusio de la Organización de Naciones Unidas para la Educación, la Ciencia y la Cultura (Unesco) 2026, el programa estatal Chiapas Puede ha logrado enseñar a leer y escribir a 250 mil personas en los 124 municipios de la entidad, en su mayoría indígenas, de 2025 a la fecha, informó Flor Marina Bermúdez, coordinadora del proyecto.
En entrevista con La Jornada, la funcionaria destacó que en promedio se destinan cada año 850 millones de pesos a la entrega de la beca Rosario Castellanos, con la que se garantizan 4 mil pesos a cada beneficiario que logra aprender a leer y escribir. Este apoyo, dijo, “es una de las acciones más efectivas para lograr que quienes no han tenido la oportunidad de escolarizarse puedan alfabetizarse”.
Indicó que por medio de un “modelo propio e innovador” de alfabetización desarrollado por el programa, que incluye la elaboración de los materiales didácticos a partir de las lenguas maternas de los alfabetizados, “hemos logrado una elevada tasa de éxito”. Enfatizó que actualmente se atiende a miles de indígenas de los cincos principales grupos lingüísticos en el estado: tseltal, tsotsil, chol, zoque y tojolabal.
Luego de ser reconocido por la Unesco como uno de los seis proyectos de alfabetización más innovadores del mundo, Bermúdez señaló que se buscó recuperar las mejores prácticas de alfabetización en América Latina para los pueblos indígenas y afrodescendientes, y “de la mano de alfabetizadores indígenas y con la visión de las etnopedagogías, coincidimos en hacer algo innovador: elaborar primero los materiales en lenguas indígenas y luego en español”.
Por ello, dijo, los libros que se usan en las comunidades no son traducciones, sino “textos auténticamente hechos por autores indígenas, que parten de la cosmovisión de los pueblos originarios, utilizando ejemplos que son comunes a éstos y las gramáticas del lenguaje, que hacen que los educandos puedan aprender primero en su lengua y luego en español”.
Se beneficiaron 165 mil mujeres
Agregó que este modelo de alfabetización ya impactó a 165 mil mujeres, en su mayoría indígenas, quienes representan 80 por ciento del total de la población que se ha logrado alfabetizar en la administración del gobernador Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar.
Precisó que en el estado se tenían detectadas entre 340 y 380 mil personas no alfabetizadas, por lo que para el año próximo se tiene la meta de alcanzar a otros 100 mil habitantes.

title: Prisoner of war's sister urges Australians to remember horrors of Sandakan
content:
Boyup Brook's vow to never forget the WWII horrors of Sandakan
In short:
The small WA town of Boyup Brook has held an annual memorial service for the victims of Sandakan Death Marches for more than 30 years.
June Edwards lost her brother Bill to the horrors of the notorious Japanese Prisoner of War camp.
The Sandakan death marches in WWII are described by the Australian War Memorial as the greatest single atrocity committed against Australians in war.
The last words 101-year-old June Edwards has from her brother Bill Beard are a scrawled note sent from the Sandakan prisoner of war camp in 1945.
Private Beard simply wrote: "Today is my birthday."
He is among the hundreds of Australian soldiers who never made it home from the notorious Japanese internment camp.
After the fall of Singapore in 1942, nearly 2,500 Commonwealth troops became Japan's prisoners of war on the Malay-Indonesian island Borneo.
In what became known as the Sandakan Death March, the Japanese forced more than 2,000 sick and weak prisoners to march 260 kilometres across Borneo in the final year of the war.
Those too weak or otherwise unable to continue were killed, with many of the bodies never recovered.
Just six soldiers survived the horrific treatment inflicted by their captors.
The local connections left a particular mark on the small town of Boyup Brook, about 260km south of Perth, which falls silent each year to remember one of the most brutal chapters in Australia's military history.
Fate shrouded in mystery
Ms Edwards said in the two years after Singapore fell, her family did not know what happened to Bill, who came from the nearby town of Worsley.
Then they received a telegram that he was a prisoner of war.
She said her mother knew her son would never return when his photo fell from the wall.
"We had hopes of him coming back," Ms Edwards said.
"But Mum said ... he'll never come back, I know from his photograph he'll never be back."
The family later discovered he had died from malaria on July 10, 1945, just a month before the end of the war.
Town's dedicated commemoration
Boyup Brook locals built a dedicated Sandakan war memorial in the early 1990s, one of the first in the country outside of Sydney.
A service is held on the second Tuesday in September each year.
Late resident and former POW Ted McLaughlin wanted to pay tribute to his good mates who died in Borneo.
When the horror of what had happened in Sandakan emerged after the war, Joe McLaughlin said his father became dedicated to ensuring those men were never forgotten.
"It took a while to find out how his mates died, and he said he must remember them,"Mr McLaughlin said.
In addition to the memorial service, the town sponsors a local student to travel to Malaysia each year, alongside historian Lyn Silver, to learn the history.
Remembrance critical
Ms Silver said the horrors of Sandakan were covered up after the war, and should never be forgotten.
"The number who died and the manner of death were so horrific," she said.
"When this was all discovered by investigators, a conscious decision was made not to give out any details to prisoners of war's families because it was too distressing."
Ms Edwards was still brought to tears at the memory of her brother, and the cruelties he suffered.
At 101, she concedes this year's service at Boyup Brook could be her last.
But she was touched to see new generations learning the history of Sandakan.
"The schools come down with their choirs and all the young ones are there," she said.
"They've got to hold them to let people know."

title: Indigenous Peoples’ Self-governance Rises to the Challenges of Today
content: Indigenous Peoples’ Self-governance Rises to the Challenges of Today tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 17:06 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Despite centuries of colonial assimilationist policies, self-governance among Indigenous Peoples is a living history that continues to unfold. And while Indigenous Peoples around the world have diverse mechanisms for self-governance, they all share the fundamental principles of an inseparable link among community, culture, and territory, as well as a collective vision of life and the exercise of power. For many Peoples this does not begin with the law, but with memory, daily practice, and the continuity of their own ways of organizing life. Self-determination is not a permission granted by the State. It is the recognition of a collective right that existed long before it was codified. Autonomy is expressed through practices passed down from generation to generation—most often orally—where dialogue, reconciliation, and communal life are real ways of making and implementing decisions. To govern is to care for collective life, the relationship with the territory, community safety, and the exercise of power. Colonizer nation States attempted to erase Indigenous Peoples’ organizational structures in favor of a homogenized identity, language, and way of living. They did not succeed in complete erasure, however. In various communities across Abya Yala, the assembly remains the space where ideas circulate and decisions are made collectively. Within it, leaders are not chosen based on popularity or purchasing power, but on their track record of service to the community. Assuming a community position entails a permanent responsibility and the obligation to be accountable to the people. Likewise, in many Indigenous communities, models of self-governance include a Council of wise people or Elders, whose role is to guide and support younger generations. This role is not acquired solely by reaching a certain age. It is based on the community’s recognition, a proven track record of service, and a life experience. Political life among Indigenous Peoples cannot be understood in isolation from territory. The care of resources, community spaces, and sacred sites is part of the very logic of governance. Justice, too, is understood from a different perspective; it is grounded in dialogue, reconciliation, and reparations. These forms of conflict resolution stand in stark contrast to colonial imperialist models that are based on punishing individuals. The coexistence of Indigenous governance systems and State structures has not been easy. Indigenous Peoples continue to operate within legal and administrative frameworks that employ complex legal and technical language and are enforced in a non-Indigenous language. When self-governance is recognized, it is typically in a partial and conditional manner. Indigenous authorities can exercise specific functions, though always within structures they do not fully control. These spaces, while important, do not equate to full autonomy. When Indigenous Peoples receive resources allocated by the State to carry out their functions, it further exacerbates the unequal power dynamic by creating mechanisms of dependency. Aymara women leaving the House of Justice after a gathering of community authorities in Chiripaca, Bolivia. Photo by Elvia Rodríguez. For a long time, States used categories such as “customs and traditions,” “local customs,” and “local practices” to refer to systems of Indigenous self-governance, thereby simplifying and diminishing them. Naming is not a neutral act: to name is to decide what is validated and what is left out. In response, Indigenous Peoples have insisted on affirming their forms of organization as their own systems of government—not only to be recognized, but also to reclaim the place that historically has been denied to them within the State. Although recognition of Indigenous self-governance has been gaining ground, putting it into practice remains fraught with obstacles. Policies aimed at Indigenous Peoples continue to be designed from a welfare-oriented and paternalistic perspective, focused more on meeting quotas than on responding to their realities, needs, and unique forms of organization, and ignoring community dynamics. All too often, the demands of Indigenous Peoples are downplayed or distorted. The case of the Māori illustrates this clearly. Their proposals for co-governance, aimed at building shared decision-making, have been labeled by some as “Māori privilege” or “ethnic elitism,” highlighting how recognition becomes contentious when it involves redistributing power. Another challenge is the inclusion of women in local governance. Attempts to increase their participation often fail to account for the burdens they already bear. Women take on community roles while simultaneously shouldering household responsibilities, doubling or tripling their workloads. For this, they are often questioned or discredited, even subjected to violence, based on patriarchal arguments rooted in exclusion. State policies have exacerbated these inequalities by failing to address the barriers women face or provide real support, shifting more responsibilities onto them without changing the underlying conditions. At the same time, Indigenous territories face the growing pressures of mining, monoculture farming, water and land grabbing, real estate developments, and tourism, leading to intensified conflicts, dispossession, criminalization, and heightened risks for those community defenders. In this context, political participation within State institutions remains limited. Even where progress has been made, such as the parliamentary representation of Māori, a fundamental question remains: to what extent does presence in these spaces translate into real participation in decision-making? Simply being present does not guarantee having an impact. The distribution of public resources has also introduced new tensions within Indigenous communities. Access to funding through government programs can generate disputes over their administration and control. In some cases, it has fostered internal divisions and corruption, consequently weakening the community fabric and complicating self-governance processes. Continuity of Indigenous Self-Governance Indigenous self-governance is not a thing of the past. It can be seen in the daily lives of various Peoples, who, despite changes and external pressures, have managed to maintain and adapt their own forms of organization within contemporary States. For them, autonomy is not an abstract idea; it is a living practice, built day by day. In Mexico, this continuity is evident in numerous regions. Data from the Oaxaca State Electoral and Citizen Participation Institute shows that 417 of its 570 municipalities are governed by Indigenous regulatory systems. More than just a statistic, this reflects the persistence of communal forms of government that continue to organize political life according to Indigenous Peoples’ own principles. In the Ñuu Savi communities, for example, the assembly remains the space where ideas are exchanged, and decisions are made collectively. There, leaders are elected, paths forward are agreed upon, and forms of accountability are established. Those who assume office are appointed based on the experience they have accumulated within community life and on the service records they have built as community members. These positions are, for the most part, unpaid, reinforcing the idea that authority is a responsibility assumed for the benefit of the people. Communal property authorities, whether agrarian or territorial administrators, demonstrate how governance and territory are deeply intertwined, particularly in the stewardship and administration of collective resources. For the Sámi Peoples in northern Europe, institutions such as the Sámi parliaments established in Norway, Sweden, and Finland have successfully created spaces for representation and dialogue with the respective States from which they participate in decisions related to their rights, cultures, and territories. These mechanisms have enabled progress toward forms of intercultural governance that incorporate Indigenous perspectives into State structures that had historically excluded them. These advances, while largely positive, also have their limits. The existence of parliaments does not imply a full transfer of power, and fundamental decisions regarding legislation or territorial management remain concentrated in the hands of the States. Even so, the Sámi experience highlights the importance of building spaces for dialogue and addressing the consequences of historical assimilation policies through truth and reconciliation processes. The cases of the Ñuu Savi, Sámi, and Māori Peoples are not isolated experiences, and demonstrate forms of governance that have persisted through their ability to adapt. Their paths have also been marked by resistance, mobilizations, and, in some cases, armed struggles that have resulted in loss of life. Faced with exclusion and dispossession, these Peoples have chosen to raise their voices and defend their rights rather than disappear in silence. Fully recognizing Indigenous Peoples entails more than creating international mechanisms and amending local laws. It requires transforming the way we understand power, territory, and life in community. In doing so, it opens the possibility of building communities where difference is not a cause for exclusion, but the foundation for a shared future. Elvia Rodríguez (Ñ’a Ñuu Savi, Ñuu Yuku Tuyuja) Is Cultural Survival Community Media Assistant.
