title: Vietnam’s nearly 400-year-old fishing village worships 2 giant whale skeletons
content:
Canh Duong Fishing Village, located in Hoa Trach Commune, is known as one of the eight ancient villages renowned for their long history in the former Quang Binh Province, which was merged with Quang Tri Province to form the new Quang Tri Province in July last year.
Historical records show that the village was founded in 1634, making it nearly four centuries old.
After hundreds of years of making a living from the sea, residents have come to see whale worship as an integral part of the village’s cultural and spiritual life.
Villagers worship two whale skeletons known as ‘Duc Ong’ (the Revered Lord) and ‘Duc Ba’ (the Revered Lady) at Ngu Linh Temple.
According to local villagers, ‘the Revered Lady’ washed ashore in the area in 1809, while ‘the Revered Lord’ came ashore in 1907.
The two enormous skeletons are displayed on wooden platforms inside the temple, with an altar standing between them.
Villagers carefully preserve numerous vertebrae, fan-shaped fin bones and skull bones.
Particularly striking are four curved ribs, each rising more than four meters against the walls.
Their immense size has led locals to compare them to giant elephant tusks.
Dao Van Hai, 69, who is responsible for looking after the temple, said that many parts of the two skeletons were lost or damaged during two wars.
In 2004, Ngu Linh Temple was built to provide a dedicated place to worship and preserve the two remaining skeletons.
Researchers previously collected samples and determined that the ‘the Revered Lord’ skeleton was some 28.8 meters long, while ‘the Revered Lady’ measured around 28.5 meters.
When alive, the two whales may have weighed hundreds of metric tons.
Not far from Ngu Linh Temple lies a cemetery reserved exclusively for whales that washed ashore along the Canh Duong coast.
Dozens of graves have been built much like human graves, each with an incense bowl placed in front of its headstone.
The headstones are inscribed with the whale’s name as well as the date when it was discovered.
Particularly intriguing is the fact that each whale grave has its own distinctive name, including Nam Duong Duke, Young Husband and Princess.
“After the whales are buried, about six or seven years later, the villagers erect stone headstones and give each grave a name,” said Nguyen Mai, a resident of Canh Duong Bac.

title: Newman Rodeo's return for first time since 2019 draws 'royalty'
content:
Return of Newman Rodeo draws 'royalty' and riders from far and wide
In short:
The small mining town of Newman has been buzzing in the lead-up to its first rodeo in seven years.
The full-points rodeo drew competitors from across the state, including rodeo royalty.
What's next?
Event organisers and locals hope the event will become a mainstay on the town's calendar.
Rodeo royalty Ariana Rhodes is among the dozens of competitors who travelled from far and wide to compete in Newman's revitalised rodeo.
Eleven-year-old Ariana and her eight-year-old cousin Svetalina Stones trotted their horses around the red dirt arena that reflects the Pilbara town's mining roots.
The pair appeared at home despite it being somewhat different to where they normally ride in Lake Clifton, south of Perth, 1,200 kilometres away.
Newman, deep in the heartland of iron ore country, has not had a rodeo since 2019.
Royalty at the red dirt rodeo
Crowned Rodeo Mini Princess last year, this is Ariana's first Newman Rodeo.
"I'm competing in barrel racing and pole bending," she said.
"My favourite's barrel racing."
Svetalina hopes to follow in her older cousin's footsteps and did not hesitate when asked about her favourite event.
"Barrel racing," she said with conviction.
Newman was the furthest she had travelled for rodeo.
The royal family lived up to their title, taking out medals for their events.
Ariana placed first in her class for barrel racing and pole bending, while Svetalina placed third in barrel racing and second in pole bending.
Talk of the town
Locals warmly welcomed the rodeo's return.
Shire of East Pilbara president Anthony Middleton said Newman had been quietly buzzing in the lead-up to the event.
"There's a fair bit of talk; it hasn't happened since before COVID," he said.
"I didn't realise how important it was to the community … it's exciting to see."
Newman Campdraft and Rodeo Association president Cameron Wilson said it was special to bring rodeo back to Newman.
"It's going to be great for the town, great for the people, and just great to see it back in Newman," he said.
Mr Hall believed the turnout would be close to 1,300 people.
"I just think it's a great exercise for the town to show what we can produce; obviously, being such a small mining town, we don't have a lot of major events," he said.
"If we can establish this and keep it a recurring thing, I think it's only going to get bigger and better year on year."
Bringing rodeo back to the Pilbara
Launching Roebourne Rodeo last year, Karlayura Rodeo co-founder Tui Magner said it made sense for Karlayura to bring rodeo back to Newman.
"Myself, Brian Tucker and Georgina Bobby have really big dreams to activate rodeos more in the Pilbara," Ms Magner said.
"Doing Roebourne Rodeo in the west Pilbara, now coming over to the east has sort of been a perfect next step to build on that success.
"Newman itself has quite a long history in rodeo … we're just really trying to build on that success."
Competitors from as far north as the Kimberley region and as far away as the South West travelled for the full-points event.
Fellow Karlayura co-founder Georgina Bobby said Newman held a special place in the Karlayura team's heart.
"This place is in Nyiyiparli country, which is Brian Tucker's mother's homeland," she said.
"I think he wanted to bring it back here for his people."
Ms Bobby highlighted the relationship between Aboriginal stockmen and modern-day rodeo.
"Back in the day, the elders, old people then, they pretty much worked on stations," she said.
"It'll be good for them to see something that's come back with this rodeo, recognising those people."

title: Country Life: Daffodil Day fundraising a farmer's legacy
content:
Daisy Groves was apparently renowned for her green thumb.
At Marangai, a 1200-hectare sheep and beef farm near Tinui east of Masterton, there are reminders of her all around the garden.
Perhaps ironically - given her name - it's the daffodils she planted through the front paddock that are her most enduring legacy.
Each year, the bright yellow blooms are picked and gifted to the local Cancer Society to help raise funds.
Green fingers, golden flowers
Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.
The tradition first started in the 1990s and has been carried on by the farm's current owners Pattie and Tony O'Boyle, owners of Marangai for close to 20 years.
"When we were negotiating to buy the farm, after some time ... we had negotiated to buy and the other party had negotiated to sell," Pattie told Country Life.
"And then the previous owner said, 'oh, hold on, one more thing'. And we were like, 'oh, no, what could this be?', and it was, would we agree to the Cancer volunteers still coming each year to pick the daffodils on the driveway, and we were like 'of course'."
It's grown into more of a community effort over the years, with friends, family, neighbours and even co-workers coming to help with the picking shortly before the annual Daffodil Day appeal.
"When we get to take them in the morning there's a big group of women [who] will be based in there just off Villa Street and they'll be bunching them for the sale and distribution and they're all just so incredibly thankful and grateful for what we bring.
"We do our best to pick the freshest ones and the more yellow ones."
There are about 11 varieties to choose from though, carpeting the steep paddock which the main driveway winds through up to the homestead.
Pattie normally tries to pick about 10 to 15 buckets - which can be filled with dozens, even hundreds of stems.
She'll also take a bucket to the previous owners, Daisy's son John Langdon, and his wife Glennis.
"They like to sort of have a reminder of, you know, their family's legacy here."
For Pattie - herself, formerly a Groves, though of no relation - it's a reminder of the caretaker role farming families play.
She described Daisy as an "avid gardener".
"Every corner of this farm she's touched something, planted something."

title: What does folklore have to say? It helps uncover untold facets of Indigenous stories overlooked for generations
content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.
As a child, I used to sit with my grandmother near a borais (a small earthen pot used to make fire) during the harsh winter days. I would listen to her stories of benevolent and malevolent characters – djinns, spirits, ghosts, witches and wizards, trees, birds and animals that had special significance in the Tharu culture and tradition. She used to sing folk songs and then explain their meaning.
I never thought of documenting the Indigenous Tharu folklore until she left this world. Now that she is no more with us, I yearn for those priceless words of wisdom. Fortunately, I had the opportunity to join hands with Amrit Sufi and Subhasish Panigrahi, who have not only been documenting oral culture in India but have also inspired and helped many culture and tradition lovers document their own cultures.
Documenting Indigenous folklore is time-consuming work. One needs to spend time with the communities before they are comfortable enough to open up and share their folktales, songs, phrases and idioms, not to mention their personal experiences.
While documenting Tharu oral culture in eastern Nepal, I came across many interesting facts that would reveal untold facets of Indigenous stories if researched further.
Morangsair: A song of seasonal migration
When I recorded a folk song called “Morangsair” or “Morangesari,” which is still sung in the eastern part of Nepal’s southern plains, I learned about the seasonal migration of young men from the Saptari District, in the easternmost part of Madhesh Province to Morang District of Koshi Province in eastern Nepal where it was more fertile and provided work for men wanting to earn some extra money.
Sunsari District, named after the Sursair River (nowadays called “Sunsari River”), was part of the Morang District before 1962. Now, we have to cross two rivers, the Koshi River and Sunsari River, to get to Sunsari (earlier Morang) from Saptari. The journey used to be much more difficult in those times, before bridges were built.
The folk song is the lament of a young woman who is pleading with her husband not to go to Morang. She talks about the dense forest, the hot climate and the Sursair River, which he would need to cross to get to Morang. However, the song doesn’t mention Koshi River, which is the biggest river in Nepal and lies ahead of Sunsari River on the way to Morang.
In the video below, Chandrakala Chaudhary from Itahari, Sunsari District, sings “Morangsair,” also called “Morangesari”:
Researching further, I learned that the current Koshi River had been flowing many kilometres east of where it is now. In the Indian part, the river has shifted almost 100 kilometres west. Also, the Ganges River is called “Sursuri” or “Sursari” in the Guru Granth Sahib, a sacred Hindu scripture. The Sursair and Koshi Rivers eventually terminate in the Ganges.
Biyahi: When a river is named after a married woman
Talking with a Tharu elder, Mahabir Chaudhary, in Nepal’s Saptari District, I came across an interesting fact: a river and its tributary have been named after the Tharu words for a married woman.
The river has been renamed “Behai” by the Nepali-speaking administrators. However, according to Tharu elders, the river’s original name is “Biyahi,” meaning the “first wife” in Kochila Tharu or Eastern Tharu language. A tributary called “Samdahi” feeds the river. Samdahi is the word for “second wife” in Eastern Tharu. The Samdahi River and Biyahi River, after the confluence, continue flowing as Biyahi River.
Sabudana ke gachhi: The tattoo motif that tells story of sago pearls
These days, sabudana or sago found in the markets is made mainly from cassava root starch. However, traditionally sago pearls were also made from the pith of sago palms. I came to find out about this process of making sago pearls during an interview with elderly Eastern Tharu-speaking women. One of them showed a tattoo that looked like a palm tree and said that it was sabudana ke gachhi. “Gachhi” is a Tharu word for a tree. She also told me that sabudana used to be made from a palm tree.
I then researched further and found that in the past they used to cut down the palm trees, scrape the starchy core from the trunk and process it further to make sago pearls. The tradition is still prevalent in some southeastern countries.
There are many more stories I have heard while documenting Tharu oral culture that need to be told to a wider audience.
But I still yearn to recall the stories told to me by my grandmother while sitting together by the fireside on chilly winter days.

title: ‘Mary Leads Us to Jesus’ — Ozigbo
content:
By Nwabueze Okonkwo
ONITSHA — Thousands of Catholics and other Christian faithful from Anambra State and neighbouring states converged on Onitsha to celebrate the birthday of the Blessed Virgin Mary, mother of Jesus Christ.
The event, organised by the Faithspiration Initiative, was themed, “Fill the Jars, Make Room for Fresh Wine,” drawn from John 2:1-11.
The celebration featured the 2026 edition of Ave Maria Praise, performances by gospel artistes, lectures, comedy, prayers and Holy Mass.
The event was held at SS. Peter and Paul Catholic Church, Iba Pope, Awada, Obosi, in Idemili North Local Government Area of Anambra State.
In his opening prayer, the parish priest, Very Rev. Fr. Dr. Aloysius Maduka Agba, prayed for the success of the celebration and journey mercies for invited guests.
Agba, who represented the chief host, the Archbishop of Onitsha, Most Rev. Valerian Maduka Okeke, described the Faithspiration Initiative as a movement comprising young people and adults, including clergy and seminarians, committed to evangelisation and promoting the gospel.
He said the birthday of the Blessed Virgin Mary was worthy of celebration because she was the mother of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of mankind.
Agba also commended the founder of Faithspiration Initiative, Very Rev. Fr. Dr. George Adimike, for his resilience and commitment to the initiative.
In his remarks, former Anambra State governorship candidate, Valentine Chineto Ozigbo, shared a testimony of what he described as a spiritual encounter during a religious event in Portugal.
Ozigbo urged Catholics to embrace Marian devotion and encourage children to pray the Rosary.
“I am not asking you to choose between Jesus and Mary. I am asking you to hold the hand of Mary so that she can lead you to her Son, Jesus Christ.
“Let us spread the Rosary and teach it to our children. Do not be ashamed of your Catholic faith. Do not be ashamed of the Mother Jesus gave us,” Ozigbo said.
He distributed rosaries to members of the congregation and provided his WhatsApp number for those interested in joining the Igbo Rosary and “Songs of Mary” platforms he created on social media.
Delivering the keynote lecture, Rev. Fr. Barr. Johnbosco Igwe, a Catholic priest and legal practitioner, spoke extensively on Marian spirituality.
He identified trust as one of the core spiritual qualities of the Blessed Virgin Mary, citing Luke 1:26-38, where Mary accepted God’s message that she would conceive and bear a child.
Igwe also highlighted gratitude, poverty, contemplation and resilience as other aspects of Marian spirituality.
In his appreciation address, the founder of Faithspiration Initiative, Fr. Adimike, thanked God and the Archbishop of Onitsha for supporting and approving the event.
He described the year’s Ave Maria Praise as outstanding and expressed optimism that next year’s edition would be bigger.
Adimike, who is known for his advocacy for the poor and needy, also commended Agba, popularly known as “Omere Ora,” for hosting the event in his parish.
“I am delighted that everybody is here to celebrate our Mother Mary — Hausas, Yorubas, and Igbos; Christians and Muslims. Everybody is invited to this feast because Our Mother Mary is a Mother to all,” he said.
He appreciated the priests, religious sisters, seminarians, sponsors and benefactors who contributed to the success of the event.
Among those acknowledged were Fr. Pharm. Evaristus Ezeani, Fr. Patrick Egaga, Fr. Simeon Enu, Fr. John Mary Iwe, Engr. Eric Anyamene, Hon. Dubem Obaze, Valentine Chineto Ozigbo, Sir Clement Onyekwelu, Sir Emeka Ezeotu and Prince Chukwuka Onyema.
Adimike also acknowledged members of the Faithspiration Initiative, including Charles Obinna Igwe, Kingsley Ezeudu, Mrs Amara Offor, popularly known as Achallugo, and Amara Dufo.
He further recognised the organisers, including the Awada CWO Zone, Mrs Ifeoma Onwugharam, President, CWO Iba Pope, Mrs Kate Amarachi, members of Catholic Women’s Organisations and Mrs Christiana Obumu Ukandu, who donated the birthday cake in honour of the Virgin Mary.
Highlights of the celebration included the cutting of the birthday cake and the distribution of food, bread and cash gifts to less privileged and vulnerable people across Idemili, Onitsha and neighbouring communities.
Gospel artistes and comedians who performed at the event included Sister Chioma Ezefeta, Sir One on One, Evangelist Onyeka Obiezu, popularly known as “Onye Amuma,” Onu Ndi Aguata and others.

title: Space Technology As a Tool for Rwanda’s Development
content:
For a long time, space technology was seen as a luxury reserved for global superpowers. And it seemed to make sense. Space infrastructure can be expensive.
In a developing country, every major investment has to compete with other seemingly more urgent development priorities. But Rwanda and a growing number of developing countries are proving that logic to be flawed. Space technology is no luxury. In fact, Rwanda is increasingly treating it as a practical tool for development.
Through the Rwanda Space Agency (RSA), the country is using satellite technology, geospatial data and other space-based services to improve public services, support better decision-making and drive economic development.
For a developing country with limited resources, the real value of investment in space technology has to be measured by what it delivers to ordinary people and how much it contributes to solving problems on the ground.
Digital connectivity is one of the clearest examples. Rwanda is exploring satellite-based high-speed internet as a way to reach communities that remain underserved by conventional broadband infrastructure.
A pilot involving 500 schools aims to give students and teachers better access to educational resources and digital tools. If scaled effectively, initiatives like this could show how technology in space can help address very terrestrial problems, such as unequal access to education and the internet.
The same is true of disaster management. Satellite data can give policymakers a much clearer picture of environmental risks, including areas vulnerable to floods and landslides. During the disasters that hit northern Rwanda in May 2023, satellite imagery helped assess the extent of the damage and inform relocation planning.
The important point here is that the value of space technology is in helping governments make better decisions, faster.
This is where the broader strategic value of Rwanda’s space programme comes in. The country is increasingly focused on turning large amounts of satellite and geospatial data into information that government institutions can actually use.
RSA is working on an indicator system designed to translate complex data into practical insights. If successful, such a system could help the government track progress on national priorities, including the National Strategy for Transformation, Vision 2050 and the Sustainable Development Goals.
That connects Rwanda’s space ambitions directly to its broader development agenda. Space-based technology can support agriculture, environmental monitoring, urban planning, infrastructure development, disaster preparedness and climate-change mitigation. In all of these areas, the goal is to use that technology to make policies more effective and public services more responsive.
Rwanda is also trying to build the infrastructure and partnerships that would allow it to play a bigger role in the regional and global space economy. A planned satellite ground station and teleport could increase the country’s ability to receive and process space-based information while creating opportunities to provide services beyond Rwanda. Its potential role in supporting lunar missions points to an even longer-term ambition: positioning Rwanda to participate in emerging markets for space-based services.
At the same time, Rwanda’s engagement with international space institutions, including its membership in the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), places its space programme within a broader framework of responsible and peaceful use of outer space.
But the real test remains whether space technology will deliver measurable economic and social benefits. That is ultimately how Rwanda’s space ambitions should be judged. Not by how many satellites it launches, how impressive its facilities look or how prominently it features in international space discussions, but by whether the technology makes life better, improves government decisions and creates new economic opportunities.
Seen this way, space technology is an extension of ordinary development policy. The broader lesson from Rwanda’s experience is simple: looking to space does not necessarily mean looking away from problems on Earth. In many cases, it means finding better tools to solve them.

title: What the commemoration of the 235th anniversary of Bois Caïman means for Haiti’s memory and future
content:
The night of August 14, 1791, marked the beginning of a series of events that changed the world. A large group of enslaved people and rebel leaders met at Bwa Kayiman (Bois Caïman), a historic site located in Haiti’s Northern Department, in the town of Plaine-du-Nord.
Under the leadership of the houngan (Vodou priest) Dutty Boukman and manbo (priestess) Cécile Fatiman — along with key resistance leaders — the gathering brought together enslaved people from different plantations for a clandestine religious and political ceremony. They invoked the lwa and ancestral spiritual forces, seeking their protection and strength for the struggle ahead.
It set in motion the first major anti-slavery movement in Saint-Domingue (which would later become Haiti), as enslaved people fought for their freedom. At that time, the island of Hispaniola was divided into two European colonies: the western part was the French colony of Saint-Domingue, and the eastern part was the Spanish colony of Santo Domingo; the modern republics did not yet exist.
During this time, Saint-Domingue was one of the world’s richest sugar and coffee colonies, built on an economy that depended entirely on the slave trade. To stop this terrible human suffering, enslaved people united to resist one of the most powerful colonial empires of the 18th century.
Coming together to resist
The resulting uprising brought together different groups of enslaved people. The population included Creole enslaved people who were born on the island, spoke Haitian Creole, understood French, and worked as skilled workers (carpenters, blacksmiths, masons, shoemakers, or house servants); “Bossales,” enslaved people who were brought directly from Africa on a négrier (slave ship), endured the hardest labour conditions and suffered brutal physical punishments, yet held onto their African roots, languages, songs, and Vodou traditions, and domestic or “elite” enslaved people who worked in the masters’ homes as servants, cooks, bodyguards, hairdressers, wet nurses, cochers (horse-drawn carriage drivers), or commandeurs (plantation slave leaders).
In this harsh environment, enslaved women often suffered sexual abuse from colonisers, which led to a mixed-race population, while plantation leaders were often forced to enforce rules with great severity. While the plantation owners tried to turn these groups against each other, the movement found strong support in les Nègres Marrons (the Maroons), who escaped the plantations and mines, and fled to the mountains to fight back.
Dehumanising treatment
During this period, plantation slaves made up the overwhelming majority of Saint-Domingue’s enslaved population, performing the most rigorous tasks and working relentless schedules from dawn until well into the night. When they arrived at colonial ports after weeks in the holds of slave ships travelling from Africa to the Americas, they were branded with heated irons as marks of identification and ownership. Branding also marked medical information or past flight attempts.
Enslaved people were routinely beaten with whips and straps made from dried cowhide, which tore through their skin and left large, bloody wounds. Other punishments included being chained in dark basements for several days, often without food. If someone rebelled, an overseer might force another enslaved person to cut off an ear, arm, or leg as a brutal deterrent to others on the plantation.
The most cruel punishments involved public hangings, beheadings, or torture. Recaptured fugitives faced these brutal penalties, and plantation mortality was high. When enslaved people grew too old or sick to perform hard labour, they were often abandoned and left to die, or executed by plantation owners who viewed them as burdens.
In stark contrast to domestic slaves and overseers, who had access to better food, agricultural and mine slaves survived mainly on water and cassava. This, coupled with the terrible labour conditions and widespread dehumanisation, ultimately fuelled the mass collective resistance that resulted in the Bois Caïman uprising.
From fight to freedom
From the mountains, these rebel fighters employed guerrilla tactics. Using weapons like slingshots, knives, machetes, and arrows, they ambushed and attacked colonial soldiers, took their weapons, poisoned water sources and animals, and burned plantations and their houses. Most of the time, these attacks took place at night, while the colonists were sleeping.
They also built a strong intelligence network. From house servants to drivers, enslaved people worked as spies to send information about hidden weapons to rebel commanders, using kònn lanbi (conch shells) and drums to send signals across the mountains. Vodou ceremonies helped prepare the fighters, who bathed in natural plant mixtures and used special powders for protection.
Following the Bois Caïman ceremony, the anti-slavery struggle continued over 12 years through the leadership of key figures such as Toussaint Louverture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Henri Christophe, Alexandre Pétion, François Capois, and Jean-Pierre Boyer. Women also played a central role in sustaining this revolution, including Marie-Jeanne Lamartinière, Sanité Bélair, Catherine Flon, and Claire Heureuse.
This movement ultimately led to the Battle of Vertières on November 18, 1803, where the insurgent army defeated the French colonial forces in the western part of Saint-Domingue. This victory brought an end to slavery in the former colony and resulted in the declaration of the first Black republic in the world — Haitian independence on January 1, 1804. Later, during the unification of the island under President Boyer in 1822, slavery was also formally abolished in the eastern Spanish-speaking side. (Under President Boyer, the Haitian government occupied the eastern part of the island, formerly Santo Domingo. This occupation began on February 9, 1822, and ended 22 years later on February 27, 1844, when the eastern side declared its independence from Haiti.)
Modern-day perspectives
To mark the 235th anniversary of this significant historic event at Bois Caïman, on August 14, 2026, various socio-cultural, Vodou, and conference/debate events were organised across the country, including an event in Cap-Haïtien organised by Kenbe Kapow, a collective founded in 2025 by a group of young people. According to Peterson Jules, Kenbe Kapow’s secretary general, who spoke with Global Voices via a WhatsApp call, it acts as an advocacy group to demand accountability from local authorities, raise civic awareness among citizens, and encourage political engagement.
In addition to political leaders, the event brought together public figures from academic, literary, and cultural sectors, and featured patriotic songs, dance performances, and discussions about the role of Bois Caïman in making Haiti the world’s first independent Black republic. Panellists also emphasised the need for national unity to address Haiti’s multi-dimensional challenges — particularly the ongoing political crisis, gang violence, and widespread public despair.
In comparing historical marronage to the country’s present-day challenges, Kenbe Kapow’s Communications Officer Karlin Georges Le Pont highlighted the importance of individual and collective responsibility:
Nou te genyen yon etap mawon, mawonaj kote esklav yo pou te ka soti sou difikilte dominasyon nan chan yo te pran chimen mòn, men yo pa t pran l pou yo te kapab deresponsabilize yo. Se te yon fòm rezistans ke moman an te mande, e pandan yo te nan mawon yo te reflechi sou kouman yo kapab pran libète yo. Si n ap eseye fè yon paralèl ak epòk sa yo, jodi a n ap viv nan yon epòk mawonaj kote ayisyen an mawon tèt li, ayisyen an mawon peyi l, ayisyen an mawon moun li ye a. Kontrèman ak ansyen mawon yo ki te mawon pou te kapab cherche libète, nou menm nou mawon paske nou di nou fatige, nou pap batay ankò. An nou soti nan etap mawonaj la pou nou vin nan etap kongrè a, etap ransebleman an ak tout fòs viv patriyòt nasyon an pou nou chita pou yon Ayiti miyò pou tout moun.
We had a stage of marronage where the enslaved, to escape the harsh domination in the fields, took to the mountains. However, they did not do so to shirk their responsibilities; it was a form of resistance required by that time. While in marronage, they reflected on how to achieve their freedom. Drawing a parallel to today, we are living in a time of modern marronage where Haitians are hiding from themselves, their country, and their identity. Unlike the former Maroons who fled to seek freedom, we flee because we say we are tired and will no longer fight. Let us move past this stage of marronage and enter the stage of the congress — a stage of gathering all the patriotic living forces of the nation to sit together for a better Haiti for everyone.
Politician and former senior state official Sterline Civil stressed the need for civic duty and action over rhetoric, noting that Haitians “must work to show that we are worthy” of the Bois Caïman heritage. “Otherwise,” she claimed, “we will never succeed and will only continue to make grand speeches.”
In a similar vein, architect and local leader Wideline Pierre emphasised the need for unity and shared purpose, suggesting that if Haitians want to emerge from the current social, political, and economic situation, they “must realise that unity, konbit (collective labor), and solidarity are what define us as a people.”
A new Bois Caïman?
Dominique Dupuy, a former minister and Haitian ambassador to UNESCO, suggested:
Se yon dezyèm Bwa Kayiman nou bezwen, se yon dezyèm chita nou bezwen, yon dezyèm gran ransebleman, yon dezyèm gwo konba nou bezwen. Se tout ayisyen nan tout orizon, patisipan yo, sa ki deyò yo, ak vwazinaj nou, zanmi nou, ak kominite nou ki ka leve jou an kò pou Ayiti, pou Ayiti zansèt yo te imajine a, pou Ayiti pitit nou yo merite a, pou yon Ayiti kote nou pap sèlman sibi jou après jou nan chèche lavi, men nan chèche lavi nou jwenn li pandan nou vivan.
We need a second Bwa Kayiman, a second sit-down meeting, a second great gathering, and a second major battle. It is all Haitians from all backgrounds, those present, those abroad, along with our neighbours, friends, and community, who can make the sun rise again for Haiti — for the Haiti our ancestors imagined, for the Haiti our children deserve, and for a Haiti where we do not merely survive day after day searching for life, but where we find life while we are alive.
Rekindling protest
On the actual historic site, the 235th anniversary commemoration involved houngans, manbos, and others from the Artibonite department — a region severely impacted by gang violence — gathering to honour their ancestors. Participants dressed in vibrant Afro-Caribbean attire adorned with vèvè symbols and portraits of lwas.
The atmosphere vibrated with the sounds of traditional instruments, including tanbou (drums), klòch (bells), and chachà (rattles). Spectators came in their numbers to the Bois Caïman grounds, where a stage and loudspeakers set the mood with traditional, rasin, and protest music.
There was a shared spirit of communion through song, dance, and protest. Marching across the site, participants carried banners bearing direct messages and demands: Ayiti pou Vodou, Vodou pou Ayiti (Haiti for Vodou, Vodou for Haiti); Aba Jezi kolon (Down with the colonial Jesus); Nou mande Leta bay peyi a sekirite (We demand that the government provide security for the country); Nou mande pou Leta retire 52/100 li bay legliz nan bidjè a (We demand that the state remove the 52 percent allocated to churches from the national budget); Jezi fè nou esklav, Desalin libere nou (Jesus made us slaves, Dessalines freed us); and Viv Ewò yo (Long live the Heroes).
Despite the historic epic achieved by Haiti’s founders who survived the transatlantic slave trade, defeated Napoleon Bonaparte’s army, and changed the course of history, the battle for true freedom is far from over.
Two hundred and twenty-two years after achieving independence, Haiti remains a unique symbol of human freedom. Yet, the nation still suffers from poverty, chronic political instability, systemic corruption, gang violence, and foreign interference.
Regardless, Haiti possesses the resources needed for its people to live with dignity as the ancestors intended, and the fight for full sovereignty, economic freedom, and social justice remains unfinished.
The greatest challenge for the Haitian people to emerge from this endemic crisis is the need for a new political and economic class, alongside a new model of civil society. This new generation of leaders must have a genuine commitment to Haiti, a clear vision, and the willingness to set personal interests aside to prioritize the nation's well-being.

title: Another plan unveiled to tackle long-standing issues in Port Augusta
content:
Taskforce to tackle crime in Port Augusta welcomed by Indigenous elders who remain critical over lack of consultation
In short:
The state government will establish a taskforce to address crime and violence in Port Augusta.
It joins a number of programs that have been attempted since the City Safe Program was axed in 2020.
What's next:
Few details on how the taskforce will function have been released with representatives from several government departments, the local member and the Port Augusta Council to discuss next steps at a closed door meeting on Friday.
Aboriginal leaders and those on the front line of Port Augusta's long-standing crime and violence issues have seen attempts to address it come and go.
As another plan is unveiled, this time a government taskforce, there is optimism but also some frustration over a lack of Indigenous consultation.
Barngarla elder Aunty Linda Dare says crime and violence is on the rise.
"As far as I'm concerned, the state needs to come and sit down with the community, because we are the ones that see it on a day-to-day basis," she said.
"They need to come and sit down, have a forum with us so we can put our opinions across to them."
For Kuyani and Adnyamathanha elder Malcolm "Tiger" McKenzie, the lack of political presence in the neighbouring Aboriginal community of Davenport is an issue that needs to be addressed.
He said repeated invitations to visit the community had been ignored.
From alcohol to illicit substances
The introduction of heavy restrictions on alcohol in 2022 was another positive step that those on the front line welcomed.
Restrictions included limits on the volume of takeaway alcohol as well as an ID scan process to ensure those limits were followed.
However, Alinda Hogg, the project coordinator at Stepping Stones – an Aboriginal drug and alcohol service provider – said the problem had shifted over the past two years as methamphetamine use increased.
She said a colleague told her a client was using methamphetamine as ID was not needed to purchase the substance.
In April this year Port Augusta Council issued a public safety notice, warning residents about the uptick in discarded needles.
Both Ms Hogg and Aunty Linda Dare said methamphetamine was fuelling more crime than alcohol now.
Danger of rhetoric stoking racism
Eli Partridge and Christian Khan, two Indigenous youth advocates, have warned that rhetoric regarding spikes in "crime", "substance abuse" or "anti-social behaviour" can turn into an attack on "young Aboriginal men".
The two 19-year-olds are both part of the Davenport Community Alliance, which was set up in late 2024.
Both say they have lived experience of being profiled, and that it has had a devastating impact on young men.
Mr Partridge says at times he's wished that his skin was lighter.
Mr Khan expressed a similar experience of feeling "ashamed of just walking around".
The pair say there was no easy answer, but praised initiatives like Mangrove Court — particularly as the program involves supporting the family units of young offenders.
"Sit with them, find out why they're doing these things, how we can remove them from that place," Mr Khan said.
History of programs in Pt Augusta
It's not the first attempt to address longstanding issues in Port Augusta.
In 2020 the Port Augusta City Safe Program was axed with the then-council stating that it was not core council business.
The program had run for 11 years, using security officers and a K9 unit to help reduce crime and violence.
Ms Hogg said it was effective at diffusing situations without needing police.
"They'd come in and calm things down … [people] didn't feel as threatened … it's not as confrontational with them," she said.
"It was pretty sad to see them go."
Aunty Linda Dare expressed similar sentiments and said there was an immediate increase in violence once the program was discontinued.
"The K9 guy, he was brilliant and I've got to give it to him," she said.
"He actually stopped a lot of fights."
In 2021 the Port Augusta Responsible Communities (PARC) was established replacing the City Safe Program.
That too lost the support of council before a government changeover in 2022 saw its end.
In 2024 $12 million was allocated for three years, from both the state and federal governments to form the Port Augusta and Davenport Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan.
There has been little detail released as to how the taskforce will function, with representatives from several government departments, the local member and council meeting on Friday to discuss next steps.
The taskforce is designed to complement the work that has already been launched by the state and federal government's Wellbeing Plan.
This includes Mangrove Court, which began in March to address the causes of youth offending.
Both elders say measures to address Port Augusta's level of crime need to have measurable KPIs that can be easily reviewed.
Breaking down barriers
Looking over the derelict buildings and overgrown sporting grounds of the long-defunct training grounds in Davenport fills Tiger McKenzie with deep sadness.
He fondly remembers how the facility and adjoining football and cricket pitch allowed Indigenous and non-Indigenous people to mingle and connect.
"They engage … those non-Aboriginal people engage with Aboriginal people to understand Aboriginal people," he said.
"Then they become mates."
Before its closure roughly 15-20 years ago, Mr McKenzie said it was a great meeting place, with teams travelling from Roxby Downs, Leigh Creek and Copley to play sport and socialise.
On nearby dunes people would "light a fire and cook kangaroo".

title: ‘Gaton – A Força da Terra’, livro de Kapri Padilha, reúne memória e resistência Kaingang
content:
Foi entre amigos, familiares, estudantes e professores que ocorreu, nesta quinta-feira (10), o primeiro de três encontros de lançamento de “Gaton – A Força da Terra”. Escrito pela indígena Kaingang Kapri Audisseia Nascimento Padilha, o livro foi apresentado na Faculdade de Educação da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), em uma atividade mediada pela filósofa Magali Mendes de Menezes. A publicação aborda a memória, a espiritualidade e a trajetória de resistência do povo Kaingang e apresenta reflexões e ensinamentos da mãe da autora, a cacica Iracema Gãh Té Nascimento, liderança política e espiritual indígena.
A autora, Kapri Padilha, explica que o incentivo para escrever o livro nasceu da trajetória da família na luta constante por direitos. “A minha inspiração foi a nossa caminhada… Ela não é fácil. A luta por território é constante e árdua, porque sempre temos que estar lutando e batalhando, mas minha mãe nunca levou para esse lado de tristeza, de briga. A força da Gâh Té me inspirou… Ela traz essa força da terra com ela. Traz a sabedoria, os nossos mitos, através dos nossos mais velhos, que é a nossa raiz”, comenta.
Outros dois eventos estão previstos para este mês. No domingo (13), o bate-papo acontecerá na Aldeia Gãh Ré, no Morro Santana, às 15h. O último encontro de lançamento ocorrerá na quarta-feira (16), no Instituto de Filosofia e Ciências Humanas da UFRGS, das 14h às 16h, com mediação da antropóloga e colaboradora do livro Geórgia Macedo. Os dois encontros terão a participação da autora e da cacica, com entrada gratuita.
Força da terra
A obra é a primeira publicação de Padilha e reflete sobre a relação dos povos indígenas com a terra, a memória e o futuro, mesclando cultura, educação e história para contar a caminhada da cacica Iracema na defesa e retomada dos territórios ancestrais e na luta pelos direitos dos povos indígenas. Ressalta, ainda, a importância de que as histórias indígenas sejam contadas pelos próprios autores e traz aspectos da cosmologia Kaingang, como a profunda relação do povo com a terra, compreendendo o território não apenas como espaço rural, mas como lugar de luta por direitos, memória, espiritualidade, ancestralidade e vida.
O livro é uma publicação bilíngue, na língua Kaingang e em português, com tradução da autora e do irmão, Adilson Karinde Nascimento Padilha. A cacica Gãh Té explica que a ideia de produzir a obra nas duas línguas surgiu da própria mistura familiar, que reúne indígenas e não indígenas. A produção envolveu a participação de integrantes do povo Kaingang, principalmente da comunidade da Aldeia Gãh Ré, onde a autora reside, no Morro Santana, em Porto Alegre, além dos territórios em São Leopoldo e Canela.
A publicação também contém fotografias do acervo pessoal da família e ilustrações dos netos da cacica Iracema, produzidas a partir da escuta das histórias da avó em oficinas de desenho.
Para a autora, tanto o processo de escrita quanto o de escolha do material que entraria na obra foram bastante desafiantes. “Eu escutava a Gãh Té e, ao mesmo tempo, escrevia. Só que a comunidade inteira estava em dúvida sobre o livro… Então ficamos sempre conversando sobre. E só depois decidimos e chamamos a professora para fazer uma oficina com as crianças. Foi um desafio, porque a gente tem tantas coisas para poder mostrar… A verdade, bem sincera, é que foi bem difícil para poder selecionar o que é mais importante porque tudo ali é importante para nós”.
A obra levou mais de dez meses para ser produzida e foi idealizada por mãe e filha, em conjunto com as antropólogas Geórgia Macedo, que colaborou na escrita, e Ana Letícia Meira Schweig, responsável pela edição e pelo projeto gráfico.
Serviço
Lançamento do livro “Gaton – A Força da Terra”, na Aldeia Gãh Ré
Quando: domingo, 13/09, às 15h
Local: Aldeia Gãh Ré (rua Natho Henn, 55, Morro Santana, Porto Alegre)
Lançamento do livro “Gaton – A Força da Terra”, com mediação de Geórgia Macedo
Quando: quarta-feira, 16/09, das 14h às 16h
Local: Sala Pantheon do Instituto de Filosofia e Ciências Humanas da UFRGS (avenida Bento Gonçalves, 9500, Porto Alegre)

title: Quais os caminhos para defender o ECA e proteger a infância
content: <_cdata>Aplicação dos princípios da lei passa por construção de uma cultura democrática baseada no respeito cotidiano aos direitos das crianças, seguindo os ensinamentos do educador Janusz Korczak A história da infância no Brasil é marcada por profundas desigualdades e sucessivas violações de direitos. Durante séculos, crianças, sobretudo negras e indígenas, foram submetidas à colonização, à escravidão, ao abandono, à falta de moradia digna, ao trabalho precoce e a diversas outras formas de violência. Essa herança permanece no racismo estrutural, nas desigualdades sociais e na dificuldade histórica do Estado em garantir proteção integral às crianças, especialmente nas periferias brasileiras. Foi para romper com essa tradição que, em 1990, o Brasil aprovou o ECA (Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente), uma das legislações mais avançadas do mundo na proteção da infância. Inspirado na Constituição Federal de 1988 e na Convenção sobre os Direitos da Criança das Nações Unidas, o Estatuto reconheceu crianças e adolescentes como sujeitos de direitos, pessoas em condição peculiar de desenvolvimento e prioridade absoluta das políticas públicas. Entretanto, 36 anos depois, persiste a pergunta: conseguimos transformar esse princípio jurídico em realidade? Os dados mostram que ainda não. Entre 2021 e 2023, o Brasil registrou mais de 15 mil mortes violentas de crianças e adolescentes, sendo 83,6% das vítimas negras. Somente em 2024, 407 crianças e adolescentes morreram em decorrência de intervenções policiais, das quais 85,1% eram negras. Mais de 18 mil denúncias anuais de violações de direitos chegam ao Disque 100, principalmente por negligência e violências psicológica e física. Mais de 60% das vítimas de estupro no país têm até 13 anos. O Unicef (Fundo das Nações Unidas para Infância) estima que 5,7 milhões de crianças e adolescentes vivem sem moradia adequada no Brasil, enquanto pesquisas da UFMG (Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais) apontam cerca de 9.000 crianças vivendo em situação de rua. Esses números revelam que a proteção prevista no ECA continua sendo profundamente desigual. Crianças não podem ser tratadas como problema, mas como prioridade ética, política e civilizatória Antes mesmo de os direitos das crianças serem reconhecidos internacionalmente, o médico, educador e escritor Janusz Korczak defendia que a criança já é uma pessoa completa, digna de respeito, participação e escuta. Sua obra influenciou a Declaração Universal dos Direitos da Criança e encontrou no Brasil importantes defensores, entre eles o jurista Dalmo de Abreu Dallari, colaborador da elaboração do ECA e tradutor da obra “O Direito da Criança ao Respeito”, publicada por Korczak em 1929. O legado do educador permanece atual porque nos lembra que proteger crianças significa construir uma cultura democrática baseada no respeito cotidiano aos direitos da infância. Nos últimos anos, o debate sobre as tecnologias digitais tornou-se indispensável. Redes sociais, inteligência artificial, cyberbullying, exposição precoce e coleta de dados exigem respostas urgentes, e o chamado ECA Digital representa um importante avanço. Porém, existe o risco de concentrarmos toda a atenção nas novas tecnologias e esquecermos que milhões de crianças continuam tendo suas infâncias roubadas por formas muito mais antigas de violência. Infâncias são roubadas a cada vez que uma criança apanha, a cada tapa naturalizado como educativo, a cada murro, a cada grito que impede a escuta e o diálogo, a cada abuso sexual silenciado dentro do quarto, a cada criança que precisa parar de estudar ou de brincar para ir vender bala no farol. Uma vida toda é roubada quando um jovem precisa deixar a universidade para trabalhar; quando a urgência do café da manhã, do almoço e da janta é mais urgente que o vestibular. A infância é roubada quando uma criança se torna mãe e, sozinha, precisa cuidar de outra criança. Também é roubada quando a violência doméstica destrói os vínculos afetivos, quando mulheres são agredidas diante dos filhos, quando crianças crescem convivendo diariamente com o medo e aprendem que a violência é uma linguagem comum das relações humanas. A infância é roubada quando o Estado se faz ausente nos territórios mais vulneráveis, oferecendo apenas respostas repressivas onde deveriam existir educação de qualidade, arte, ciência, cultura, esporte, saúde, assistência social, transporte público gratuito, acesso à cidade e às oportunidades de desenvolvimento pessoal e comunitário. A infância é roubada quando crianças e adolescentes são privados do direito de desenvolver pensamento crítico, autonomia intelectual e participação cidadã. Uma democracia depende da formação de sujeitos autônomos, conscientes e capazes de dialogar com a diversidade. Toda forma de manipulação ou negação desse direito compromete não apenas o desenvolvimento individual, mas a própria democracia. Antes do crime, muitas vezes houve abandono. Antes da punição, houve omissão coletiva. Uma sociedade que abandona suas crianças não possui legitimidade ética para cobrar segurança pública. Crianças precisam de escolas de qualidade, professoras e professores valorizados, espaços verdes, cultura, artes, esporte e oportunidades de desenvolvimento, não de prisões. A penitenciária é um dos maiores exemplos da presença do racismo ainda nos dias de hoje na concepção e política de justiça. Por isso, propostas como a redução da maioridade penal não contribuem para enfrentar as causas estruturais da violência. Deslocam o debate para a punição e ignoram desigualdades históricas, raciais, econômicas e educacionais que atingem principalmente a juventude negra e periférica. Mais de três décadas após sua promulgação, o desafio do ECA não é apenas responder às novas violências digitais, mas cumprir aquilo que determina desde 1990: garantir proteção integral, prioridade absoluta e igualdade de oportunidades para todas as crianças. Experiências desenvolvidas por educadoras, educadores, escolas e projetos sociais demonstram que a efetivação desses direitos depende da articulação permanente entre sociedade e Estado. A legislação, sozinha, não transforma a realidade; ela precisa ser acompanhada por políticas públicas consistentes, financiamento adequado e compromisso coletivo. Defender o ECA é reconhecer que crianças não podem ser tratadas como problema de segurança pública, mas como prioridade ética, política e civilizatória. Como ensinava Janusz Korczak, a qualidade de uma democracia pode ser medida pela forma como trata suas crianças, pela forma como as crianças ocupam e participam dos espaços e da vida pública. Enquanto houver uma criança submetida à violência, ao racismo, à fome, ao abandono, ao trabalho infantil, à exclusão escolar ou à negação de seus direitos, a promessa inaugurada pelo ECA permanecerá incompleta. Fortalecer e atualizar o estatuto significa reafirmar o compromisso do Brasil com a dignidade humana, a justiça social e a construção de uma verdadeira cultura de proteção às infâncias. Não se trata apenas de proteger crianças, mas de decidir que sociedade desejamos construir para que elas não sejam punidas pelos crimes cometidos contra suas infâncias. Para tanto, podemos nos inspirar e aprender com a tradição e a sabedoria das aldeias e dos quilombos como referências fundantes da nossa história e territórios, dentro de uma perspectiva cultural diversa, plural, democrática e científica. Denis Plaper é cientista social e professor licenciado pela PUC-SP (Pontifícia Universidade Católica de São Paulo) e mestre em filosofia da educação pela Faculdade de Educação da USP (Universidade de São Paulo). É coordenador pedagógico, tendo atuado no Programa de Desenvolvimento Docente da FGV-SP (Fundação Getulio Vargas de São Paulo)

title: Desolador panorama del trato que reciben los jóvenes indígenas en el sistema de justicia australiano
content:
Este artículo es parte de la serie Spotlight de Global Voices de agosto “Derechos indígenas”. Esta serie ofrece una visión de las vidas y experiencias de los pueblos indígenas, de las conexiones a través de regiones, experiencias indígenas y contar las historias de líderes, activistas y miembros de la comunidad y más. Puedes apoyar este reportaje con una donación.
Mientras los activistas continúan luchando por eliminar la desigualdad en la comunidad indígena en Australia, una reciente actualización de la Comisión de Productividad del Gobierno australiano muestra un panorama sombrío de la desigualdad dentro del sistema de justicia, sobre todo para los jóvenes indígenas. El informe es parte del Acuerdo Nacional para Cerrar la Brecha, que busca «hacer posible que los aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres y los Gobiernos trabajen juntos para dejar atrás la desigualdad que viven los aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres y lograr resultados de vida iguales a los de todos los australianos».
El informe señaló que la detención de indígenas está en aumento, mientras que hay una enorme desproporción de jóvenes de las Primeras Naciones en el sistema penitenciario australiano:
The rate of First Nations prisoners jumped to more than 2,500 per 100,000 adults in 2025 and up from more than 2,300 a year earlier and more than 550 in 2019.
… First Nations youths remain heavily over-represented in detention, with 25.7 children aged 10–17 per 10,000 in custody on an average day in 2024-25 and ‘‘no change from the baseline’’ towards the target of a 30 per cent cut by 2031.
El índice de prisioneros de las Primeras Naciones pasó a más de 2500 cada 100,000 adultos en 2025, de más de 2300 un año antes y más de 550 en 2029.
…los jóvenes de las Primeras Naciones siguen siendo abrumadora mayoría en las detenciones, con 25,7 niños de entre 10-17 años cada 10,000 en arrestados en un día promedio entre 2024 y 2025.
El Servicio Legal para Aborígenes e Isleños del Estrecho de Torres resaltó que, en comparación con el promedio de otras poblaciones, a los jóvenes de las Primeras Naciones lo detienen sin sentencia mucho más tiempo:
The average length of time spent in unsentenced detention was 57.2 days, with the highest average in Queensland at 96.3 days and Victoria at 81.1 days.
El promedio de tiempo de arresto sin sentencia fue de 57.2 días; el promedio más alto es el de Queensland con 96.3 días y Victoria con 81.1 días.
El gerente general del Servicio Legal para Aborígenes e Isleños del Estrecho de Torres, Nick Espie, fue incisivo con los últimos hallazgos:
The data shows that yet again, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children — who have had no finding of guilt against them — are being locked up at alarming rates and for alarming amounts of time.
The evidence is clear that when a child spends time behind bars, it increases their likelihood of reoffending. Not only is this approach cruel and damaging to our children and their families, governments are spending almost AUD 3,200 on locking up children, a measure we know makes communities less safe.
Los datos muestran que, una vez más, los niños aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres —a quienes no se los ha declarado culpables de ningún delito— son detenidos a un ritmo alarmante y por una preocupante cantidad de tiempo.
La evidencia es clara. Cuando un niño pasa tiempo tras las rejas, aumenta la probabilidad de reincidencia. No solo este planteamiento es cruel y perjudicial para nuestros niños y sus familias, los Gobiernos están gastando casi 3200 dólares australianos en encerrar niños, una medida que sabemos que hace mas inseguras a las comunidades.
En mayo de 2026, la Oficina de Derechos Humanos de Naciones Unidas se refirió a este problema y destacó que:
The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination today expressed alarm over the persistent overrepresentation of Indigenous children in Australia’s criminal justice system, warning that this reflects systemic and structural racial discrimination against Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
… In several states and territories in Australia, the minimum age of criminal responsibility is lower than the threshold under international human rights law and standards, and in some cases is as low as 10 years old.
Hoy, el Comité para la Eliminación de la Discriminación Racial de la Naciones Unidas ha expresado alarma acerca de la gran desproporción de niños indígenas en el sistema de justicia penal australiano, y advierte que esto refleja discriminación sistémica y estructural contra las comunidades aborígenes e isleñas del Estrecho de Torres.
… En varios estados y territorios de Australia, la edad mínima de imputabilidad es más baja que el límite bajo la ley internacional de derechos humanos, y en algunos casos llega a los 10 años.
El Servicio Legal para Aborígenes e Isleños del Estrecho de Torres fue una de las más de 200 organizaciones que firmaron una carta abierta para el primer ministro australiano, Anthony Albanese, que llamaba al Gobierno a tomar acción de manera urgente:
From coast to coast across our lands, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are being criminalised and imprisoned at alarming rates because of political point-scoring rather than evidence-based reforms.
This is an emergency.We… are urging you to call an emergency summit on youth justice, so that key decision makers in government can listen to the voices of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander legal experts and leaders in a setting where community-controlled organisations lead the discussion.
De costa a costa a lo largo de nuestra tierra, a los niños aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres se les criminaliza y encarcela a un ritmo alarmante por buscar rédito político en lugar de reformas hechas con datos contrastados.
Esta es una emergencia.Los instamos a convocar a una cumbre de emergencia para darle justicia a los jóvenes, para que quienes toman decisiones en el Gobierno puedan escuchar las voces de los expertos legales y líderes aborígenes e isleños del estrecho de Torres en un ámbito donde las organizaciones controladas por la comunidad dirijan la discusión.
Amnistía Internacional Australia inició su campaña Kids Need Better en agosto de 2026, que pide justicia por los jóvenes indígenas:
Únete a a la nueva era de nuestra campaña de justicia para los jóvenes indígenas.
————-
📣¡Esta noche es la gran noche! ¡Confirma tu asistencia en el enlace en la biografía!Nos vemos en línea esta noche para escuchar al tío Rodney Dillon, a Kacey Teerman, a Anne Hollonds y a Satara Uthayakumaran.
Acompáñanos mientras damos a conocer la visión detrás de la campaña, lo que hemos aprendido al trabajar junto a las comunidades de las Primeras Naciones, nuestros simpatizantes y expertos, y cómo juntos podemos construir un futuro en el que cada niño sea tratado con dignidad y humanidad.
Rodney Dillon, anciano de la Nación de Palawa en lutruwita (Tasmania), presentó la campaña en este video:
El video presenta algunas soluciones que llevarían al sistema penitenciario de Australia a ser más justo:
We’re calling on governments to establish enforceable minimum standards for the treatment of children in custody, raise the age of criminal responsibility to at least 14, invest in Indigenous-led community solutions, and end harmful detention practices. Because every child deserves dignity, care and the opportunity to thrive.
Pedimos que los Gobiernos establezcan parámetros mínimos ejecutables para el trato de los niños detenidos, que aumenten la edad de imputabilidad a los 14 años como mínimo, que inviertan en soluciones comunitarias y que detengan las prácticas de detención dañinas. Porque los niños merecen dignidad, cuidados y la oportunidad de prosperar.
La petición en línea de Amnistía Internacional destaca algunas novedades de algunos Gobiernos y estados. Por ejemplo:
In the Northern Territory, the minimum age a child can be imprisoned has been lowered to 10, spit hoods have been reintroduced, and children continue to be held in overcrowded youth detention centers and police watch houses. Almost every child in detention is First Nations.
En el territorio norte, la edad mínima de imputabilidad en la que un niño puede ser detenido bajó a 10 años, han vuelto a usar capuchas antisaliva y a los niños los siguen deteniendo en comisarías y en centros de detención para jóvenes que están sobrepoblados. Casi todos los niños detenidos son de las Primeras Naciones.
Las capuchas antisaliva son riesgosas y hasta mortales, y fueron prohibidas en el territorio norte junto con las sillas de sujeción luego de una escándalo nacional en 2017, pero luego fueron restablecidas en 2025.
En 2025, el informe de la Comisión de Derechos Humanos australiana, «Help Way Earlier!», mostró un panorama perturbador de cómo el sistema de justicia australiano maltrata a los niños:
On an average day, 4,542 children across Australia were under youth justice supervision.
57 percent were Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children
Indigenous children were 23 times more likely to be under supervision and 28 times more likely to be in detention than non-Indigenous children
En un día promedio, 4542 niños en Australia están bajo supervisión de la justicia juvenil.
El 57% son niños aborígenes e isleños del Estrecho de Torres.
Los niños indígenas son 23 veces más propensos a estar bajo supervisión y 28 veces más propensos a ser detenidos que los niños no indígenas.
Los principales hallazgos incluyen:
Many children in contact with child justice systems have experiences of poverty, violence, abuse, intergenerational trauma, mental health issues, homelessness, drug and alcohol abuse, and neurodevelopmental disabilities.
Many are in the child protection systems or living in out-of-home care.
If children at risk are supported earlier on — whether in the community, in detention, or when released from detention — they are less likely to be involved in criminal activity, keeping them and our communities safe.
Muchos niños en contacto con los sistemas de justicia infantil viven la pobreza, violencia, abuso, trauma intergeneracional, problemas de salud mental, situación de calle, adicción a las drogas y al alcohol, y discapacidades de desarrollo neurológico.
Muchos están en el sistema de protección de menores o viven bajo tutela fuera del hogar.
Si los niños en riesgo tienen apoyo temprano —ya sea en la comunidad, durante su detención o cuando son liberados— es menos probable que terminen involucrados en actividades delictivas, preservando su seguridad y la de las comunidades.
Anne Hollonds, ex comisionada nacional para la infancia de Australia, explicó el informe en este video:
Estos informes sostienen firmemente que las medidas duras y punitivas no están funcionando. Detener un niño por un año cuesta un millón de dólares australianos (700,000 dólares estadounidenses), y los detractores argumentan que es momento de intentar algo diferente.
Aunque algunos estados tienen diferencias y otras iniciativas para reducir las detenciones de jóvenes indígenas, los activistas aseguran que no hay progreso suficiente para reducir esta vergüenza nacional.
El senador Malarndirri McCarthy, ministro federal para los indígenas australianos, urge a los Gobiernos estatales y territorios a hacer más.
State and territory governments must also back in their commitments under the National Agreement with investments and policies that improve outcomes for First Nations people.
Los Gobiernos estatales y territoriales también deben respaldar sus compromisos en virtud del Acuerdo Nacional con inversiones y políticas que mejoren la situación de los pueblos de las Primeras Naciones.
La presentación del seminario web de la campaña de Amnistía Internacional incluye pedidos de jóvenes en prisión en Australia. Se puede ver el video de 50 minutos debajo.

title: Indigenous community trades shark-fishing for conservation in Colombia: 'From hunter to protector'
content:
- In the Colombian department of La Guajira, at South America’s northernmost tip, Indigenous Wayuu fishers from the community of Punta Gallinas are working with marine biologists to conserve and document shark populations.
- Despite a 2021 law banning targeted shark and ray fishing in Colombia, the meat remains a vital protein source in one of the country’s most remote and food-insecure regions.
- Colombian shark conservation initiative Proyecto Puyuii is working with Wayuu fishers to record shark species in the understudied waters of La Guajira, implementing sustainability measures such as larger-mesh nets, safe release techniques, and avoiding longlines.
- With sustainable tourism touted as a potential economic alternative to shark fishing, some fishers argue that compensation will need to be offered before they can afford to stop.
LA GUAJIRA, Colombia — Feet from the ocean, four sharks and a ray lie dead on the wind-battered sand. Above them stands Wilfrido Arends, 46. The blade of a short knife glints in his hand.
Carefully, he bends down to cut a small fin from the underside of one shark — an endangered species known as a blacknose (Carcharhinus acronotus). He hands the sample to a woman next to him, who places it delicately in a vial.
A tape measure is passed over the still glistening back of the dead shark. Each measurement is read out and noted down.
Arends, a fisher from Colombia’s Wayuu Indigenous community, is spearheading shark research and conservation in Punta Gallinas, a Wayuu community where shark meat is part of the traditional diet. Home to around 50 families, the community sits at the northernmost tip of South America.
“If we wipe out our sharks, I think that further down the line we will miss them,” says Arends, who is known locally as “Caracas.”
Together with researchers from Colombian shark conservation initiative Proyecto Puyuii, Arends and other Wayuu fishers are documenting shark diversity in the largely unstudied waters of La Guajira.
“There’s almost no data on anything,” says Diego Cardeñosa, a marine biologist at Florida International University in the United States. A member of Proyecto Puyuii, he has been training Wayuu fishers to record the shark species they catch.
A 2021 law banned shark and ray fishing in Colombia, with a 2024 revision subsequently allowing the incidental bycatch of 15 species. Despite the ban, the meat remains an important source of protein for Wayuu communities across this stretch of arid desert coast — one of the most food-insecure regions in the country.
While commercial poaching is the leading threat to shark populations in Colombia, biologists say that without additional research, even traditional subsistence hunting can increase pressure on sharks, possibly affecting their numbers or threatening endangered species — as happened with overconsumption of turtles.
Proyecto Puyuii aims to promote economic alternatives for fishers, minimize pressure on the local shark population with scientific research, and implement sustainable fishing practices.
The consumption of sharks is accepted by the project, as it is a traditional practice and form of subsistence. But directed shark fishing (generally practiced with longlines in the deeper ocean) is not encouraged. A more sustainable model would limit consumption to incidental bycatch, which depending on the species is not illegal, and include safe release techniques of juveniles.
“If the fisher earns more showing it than killing it, there’s the solution,” says Felipe González, who co-founded the project with Arends over a decade ago. “How do we make these sharks worth more alive than dead?”
‘I gave up shark-directed fishing many years ago’
Like many Wayuu boys in the region, Arends began fishing at the age of 9. As a child, he watched his grandparents hunt shark species ranging from hammerheads to tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier).
“As I got older I took to fishing them too, because it was a custom of the Wayuu,” says Arends, who recalls participating in a once booming trade that saw shark meat and fins exchanged for money, fuel, or resources with buyers in neighboring Venezuela.
“You’d sell it and buy fuel to keep fishing,” he remembers. “We’d buy nets and hooks. That’s how we kept ourselves going.”
At this time, fishers in Punta Gallinas would use artisanal longlines specialized for shark fishing, as well as finer-mesh gillnets that result in higher levels of shark bycatch. According to Arends, the trade began to disappear from Punta Gallinas over a decade ago, before vanishing from the community with the 2021 prohibition.
Local fishers told Mongabay that other Wayuu communities do still participate in a market, with buyers from the towns of Riohacha and Uribia paying around 50,000 Colombian pesos (about $15) per kilo for shark fins.
Though the fin trade is absent in Punta Gallinas, shark meat is still commonly consumed in the community, forming the key ingredient in a traditional dish known as salpicón. Oil is also extracted from the carcasses and used for cooking, while the liver is used in the production of a traditional cough medicine.
Whatever meat is not consumed by the fisher’s own family is typically sold to locally owned hotels and restaurants. Biologists have not assessed the mercury levels (which could be harmful at high concentrations) of shark meat in Punta Gallinas. González says it may be low and is currently not a concern of the project.
“It’s an important protein source,” Arends says, “the first source we have here to feed ourselves and our children is shark.”
Despite the ongoing subsistence use in his community, Arends is determined to promote shark conservation.
“Now I fish mostly with nets — I’ve stopped using what we call the longline, because that fishing is more directed at sharks,” he says. “I gave up shark-directed fishing many years ago.”
Since the early 2000s, Arends has worked on community-based mangrove and sea turtle conservation. Locals report that sea turtles, once a common sight, have disappeared from the area due to overconsumption in local Wayuu communities.
“What happened with the turtles — we don’t want the same thing to happen with the sharks,” he says.
He and other Punta Gallinas fishers began to use large-mesh nets to avoid catching juvenile sharks, focusing instead on other fish species by placing nets away from the open sea, where sharks are commonly found.
If he catches a shark incidentally, it will be released if found alive.
Locals report that these measures have been widely adopted in Punta Gallinas. And, according to Arends, around 17 boats out of an estimated 20 in the community no longer practice shark-directed fishing. Numbers aren’t available on how many have also changed to larger-mesh nets.
“You feel like your programming has been changed — from hunter to protector,” he says. “You feel almost the same as what the animals feel.”
‘A high concentration of shark species’
Though still largely understudied, biologists believe that the waters around Punta Gallinas are likely to contain a wealth of shark diversity.
“In La Guajira and other parts of the Colombian Caribbean, there appears to be a high concentration of ray and shark species,” says Camilo Garcia, professor of marine biology at the National University of Colombia, who mapped the distribution of sharks and rays across the Colombian Caribbean using research data from as far back as the 1960s.
Though his work identified a total of 90 species, he describes the inventory as “incomplete” and believes that further research is needed to establish sustainable catch levels and ensure the sustainability of current and future fishing practices.
In Punta Gallinas, Wayuu fishers have reported the presence of species ranging from tiger and silky sharks to endangered blacknose and the critically endangered smalleye hammerhead (Sphyrna tudes).
Cardeñosa believes that Proyecto Puyuii’s drive to document shark species is a crucial step toward facilitating more informed conservation measures in the future, such as fishing quotas and conservation areas.
As part of the project, Wayuu fishers measure every shark they catch, with dated fin samples passed to Arends for storage.
“This is going to give us a bigger picture of the species composition of the fishery, how much they’re catching and whether it can be sustainable,” Cardeñosa says. “Then we can start to formulate more advanced projects.”
‘What are we going to live off?’
Amid mounting food and water insecurity across La Guajira’s desert coast, a potential transition away from shark fishing is a challenging proposition for some communities. The Wayuu fishers Mongabay spoke to generally consider the 2021 law unfair on communities that still subsist on shark.
Locals report that a lack of rain in 2025’s wet season resulted in widespread plant and livestock death. Luzmila Arends, sister of Wilfrido, reports losing around 247 of her 300 goats after the failed rainy season left little vegetation to feed them. Goats are another common source of meat in Wayuu communities.
Meanwhile, one in three children in the region suffers from chronic malnutrition.
“Many people live off of shark meat,” says Juan Manuel Uriana, 33, leader of the fishers’ association in Bahía Hondita, a larger Wayuu community about 4 miles from Punta Gallinas. “Since there’s no other way for people to live, they do it to survive … they know it’s a crime now.”
According to Uriana, many of the 120 fishers in Bahía Hondita use hooks and longlines to catch sharks and rays, a trade they still rely on for survival.
“You have to compensate people. Then they would stop fishing shark,” he says. “What are we going to live off?”
Proyecto Puyuii members hope that sustainable tourism can provide alternative opportunities. The project is currently affiliated with a Wayuu-run hotel and kite surfing school in the area, a short drive from the famous Taroa sand dunes — a renowned beauty spot.
“The idea is that the money stays in the community,” González says, “that the tourist arrives, sleeps in their guesthouse, eats what they prepare, uses their boats and their guides.”
For some in Punta Gallinas, this has already become a reality.
“I’m earning more now,” says Alexi López, 56, uncle of Wilfrido Arends. Once one of Punta Gallinas’ most prolific shark fishers, he now makes most of his living driving cars and boats for tourists. “It’s easier [than fishing] because I go out, am done in two hours and am back home again.”
Luzmila Arends runs a local guesthouse, which offers visitors the chance to accompany fishers on boat outings.
She hopes that economically viable alternatives will help the community to shift away from a historical dependence on shark meat.
“It’s all culture,” she says. “It’s not that we talk today and tomorrow it’s done, but that people go forwards with that vision for the future. It won’t happen overnight.”
‘Better we release them’
Even amongst those who live off shark fishing, there is evidence of a growing willingness to protect what remains.
“If this project works out, we can participate in conservation, we can work with this,” Uriana says. “The people are open to it.”
In May 2026, fishers in Bahía Hondita caught a large female tiger shark. On opening the animal, they found that it was pregnant. “One of the boys was going to gather [the pups] to take them away,” Uriana says. “I said: no, why are you going to take them? Better we release them.”
According to marine biologists, the protection of young sharks is of particular importance for a sustainable fishery. “More dangerous is fishing juveniles,” Garcia says. “If you catch them, especially before they’ve reproduced, you’re destroying the population directly.”
Using safe release techniques learned from Proyecto Puyuii, Uriana released 43 living tiger shark pups into the ocean.
He speaks from behind dark glasses and the low brim of a cap. “We started releasing them with the children,” he says.
A group of young boys, aged between 8 and 12, watches on as he talks. Uriana gestures to them. “They already know how to fish,” he says.
Back on his fishing boat, Wilfrido Arends scans the horizon, one hand guiding the onboard motor at the rear. A ragged black flag, marking the position of his net, appears from behind the crest of a wave.
Without a word, his 22-year-old son moves to haul it into the boat. He is nicknamed “Caraquitas” (“Little Caracas”) after his father.
“Everything we’ve tried to do is to leave something for our children,” says Arends, whose granddaughter and one of his sons want to become marine biologists. Arends, himself, dreams of one day establishing a shark research center in Punta Gallinas.
“Our ancestors have left this to us,” he says. “We want to leave something better for those who come next.”
This article was originally published on Mongabay.
