title: Meals, transit, and trust helped one California school end chronic absence for unhoused students
content:
At Scholarship Prep South Bay in Wilmington, Calif., school leaders say an attendance strategy centered on basic needs, trust, and community care helped ensure that no student experiencing homelessness at the charter school was chronically absent — an unusual result in a state where unstable housing often contributes to repeated missed school days.
Here's what to know
The school served 421 students, including 54 who were experiencing homelessness, according to the Los Angeles Times. Scholarship Prep South Bay spans transitional kindergarten through eighth grade, and nearly 93% of its students come from low-income families.
Support at the school extends well beyond academics. Students receive meals, before- and after-school care, uniforms, hygiene supplies, on-campus health and wellness services, and access to washers and dryers. Families can also get weekly food boxes, grocery assistance, hotel help, and Metro GoPass TAP cards for transportation.
Scholarship Prep chief executive and co-founder Jason Watts said the model is both simple and far-reaching, per the Times: "We create a school where everyone is welcome, cares about students and families, has incredible wraparound services, gives students what they need — and they stay."
California data show a sharp difference in absenteeism rates. About 35% of students experiencing homelessness are chronically absent statewide, compared with 19% of students overall. Studies from the UCLA Center for the Transformation of Schools found that the number of homeless students in Los Angeles County increased from 47,689 in the 2022-23 school year to 61,249 in 2023-24.
More background
Trauma-informed support is part of the school's everyday approach. Staff members are trained to help children who have experienced trauma, and social and emotional learning is built into daily classroom lessons.
Kristen Crowe, the school's chief community officer, said that approach begins with dignity.
"We lead with love and respect," Crowe said, per the Times, describing a family resource center focused on belonging rather than judgment.
Each classroom has a "rainbow cart" stocked with basics such as deodorant, toothbrushes, toothpaste, hair care products, and school supplies. The school also starts the day with a morning meeting so teachers can check in and get a sense of how students are doing.
According to the Times, Jace, a 14-year-old eighth grader, said, "My favorite thing about being here is that the teachers are very friendly, and you get to connect with them. They're very helpful also, no matter if you need support with a specific subject, whether it's outside of school or not."
What's being done?
To keep the support system in place, Scholarship Prep South Bay says it works with more than 50 community partners. Those partnerships help supply food, school materials, hygiene kits, counseling, and other services meant to reduce the barriers that can keep children out of class.
Students also have access to calming corners in their classrooms, stocked with breathing exercise instructions, fidgets, stress balls, and noise-canceling headphones. If they need more time to reset, they can spend 10 minutes in a mental health room to decompress.
Spring 2025 state test results show the school still has areas to improve, especially in math. The paper noted that those comparisons may not fully reflect the school's circumstances, given its high share of low-income and homeless students and the challenges of frequent student mobility.
"Loving the whole child includes the family," said Principal Allison Vann, the Times reported.
Jennifer Friend, CEO of Project Hope Alliance, added, "Our greatest impact is by investing in today's students experiencing homelessness. Every day I get to watch our youth show up powerfully, and that is an investment well placed," per the Times.
Where can I learn more?
Supporting student engagement usually starts with addressing basic necessities, such as reliable transit and nutrition, while fostering an encouraging environment on campus. Across different communities, schools are enriching student experiences through accessible meals, eco-friendly transportation, and interactive initiatives that build strong connections.
• Teachers and parents organized food collections, put out for families after school.
• In Oakland, the district made a groundbreaking decision to electrify buses for cleaner rides.
• Teachers harnessed children's curiosity to help inspire school composting and cut cafeteria waste.
By fostering a welcoming environment and simplifying daily routines, schools create the foundation students need to attend consistently. Scholarship Prep South Bay's impressive attendance progress reflects the power of this dedicated approach.

title: Woolly dog pelt returns to Coast Salish territory for the first time
content:
Woolly dog pelt returns to Coast Salish territory for the first time
The only surviving woolly dog pelt tells a story of vibrant cultural values
His name was Mutton. Although he died in 1859 at the tender age of 18 months, Mutton is a survivor who has returned to his ancestral territory to be studied, and welcomed with respect by Coast Salish artisans and community members.
Mutton, a woolly dog, whose hair was used in Salish and Makah weaving, was the companion of naturalist and ethnographer George Gibbs, who worked on the Northwest Boundary Survey in the 19th century.
Mutton’s pelt, the only surviving pelt of the woolly dog, is on loan to the Museum of Anthropology at the University of B.C. from the Smithsonian Institution until August 2027.
In his field notes, Gibbs recorded that Mutton grew ill and died around 1859. Those notes, and the pelt, along with other wildlife specimens, were sent to the Smithsonian at the end of the expedition Gibbs was part of. The pelt was carefully preserved, but lay forgotten in a drawer until it was rediscovered around the year 2000.
Jordan Wilson, curator of Pacific Northwest and Contemporary Indigenous Art at the Museum of Anthropology, unveiled the pelt on Tuesday, after local Indigenous community members had time to visit and spend time with their returning canine ancestor.
The woolly dog, which has a fox-like face and a brown button nose, appears in rare historical photographs, in sketches by artist Paul Kane, and on woven Skokomish/Twana baskets. But the breed itself vanished some time around the late 1800s.
Stories of a fluffy, white dog whose soft fur was sheared and collected like wool to be used in traditional weaving, have been passed down through oral traditions by Coast Salish community members for over 100 years since its disappearance.
“This is the only existing pelt of a now-extinct breed of dog that was once selectively bred here in the Coast Salish region and the neighbouring territories of the Interior Salish and the Makah people. Our ancestors bred these dogs for their fur to be used in weavings, robes and other textiles,” said Wilson.
“Early historical accounts from Capt. George Vancouver and Simon Fraser make reference to Indigenous peoples travelling in canoes with woolly dogs, so we have a sense that the dogs travelled with our ancestors as they moved throughout their respective territories,” said Wilson.
The pooches were kept separate from other village dogs so their beautiful pelts would not be compromised by cross-breeding to preserve the integrity of their fleece. “There was a very selective breeding process that ensured the quality of the fur,” said Wilson.
According to a study published in the research journal Science in 2023 after Mutton’s genome was sequenced, the dogs had a distinctive curly undercoat. They were pampered, regarded as “people,” “relatives” and members of the family, loved and cared for, combed, and fed a special diet of salmon.
Genomic testing on Mutton and other breeds from Coast Salish territories show that woolly dogs were present for at least 5,000 years before European colonization, possibly up to 15,000 years.
The woolly dogs were much more than companions. Their cloud-like hair was spun and woven into traditional blankets, supplementing other materials such as waterfowl down and fluff from plants like cattails and fireweed.
According to Debra Sparrow, a Musqueam master weaver, her grandfather Ed Sparrow told her that, “Every village had (woolly dogs), that they were like gold because they were mixed with the mountain goat and then rove and spun.”
“Research is still ongoing doing testing on existing Salish blankets and other weavings,” said Wilson.
Settler colonialism impacted the way of life that protected these pups, including the management of their breed. They did not survive the social conflicts and cultural interruptions that came with the Gold Rush, the establishment of the Indian Act, the potlatch ban, and assimilation.
The significance of this pelt isn’t just about the extinction of a species, said Wilson. “It also speaks to the lives of our ancestors, their relationship with the more-than-human world, and their teachings and knowledge that continue to be passed forward.”

title: Kottayam to King's College: UK nurse shares journey of winning Aster Guardians Award
content:
Kottayam to King's College: UK nurse shares journey of winning Aster Guardians Award
Dr Agimol Pradeep co-founded Upahaar, which registered over 10,000 organ and stem cell donors. She now plans to invest half her prize in the initiative
- PUBLISHED: Sat 12 Sept 2026, 9:23 PM
Nurse Dr Agimol Pradeep was on duty the day a young woman in her late 20s with liver failure was brought in, close to death. A transplant was her only hope. By chance, or by the Almighty’s grace, Dr Agimol was the on-call transplant coordinator when a match was found.
She escorted the girl to theatre, then cared for her through recovery. he girl survived and made a choice that would shape Dr Agimol's career. "She then decided to be my patient advocate when we go out in the community to promote organ donation," Dr Agimol recalled, speaking to Khaleej Times from the southern Indian state of Kerala. "She will always be with me in the journey, reminding me why I do this job."
Dr Agimol, a Senior Transplant Coordinator at King's College Hospital, was sharing her experience just moments after being named winner of the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award 2026 in a grand ceremony that took place in the metropolitan city of Kochi. "Winning an award, representing my home country, India, in my birth land, Kerala, is beyond any imagination," she said.
Stay up to date with the latest news. Follow KT on WhatsApp Channels.
Since its launch in 2021, the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award has grown into a global platform that celebrates nurses who are advancing the profession and creating meaningful change. This year drew over 134,000 registrations from 214 countries, bringing forward stories of nurses working across different healthcare settings, communities and disciplines.
Dedicating her work
That moment with the young woman was a turning point in Dr Agimol’s life. It was the start of her career built on noticing what others overlook. Early in her work, she saw that South Asian patients were dying while waiting for transplants, because too few donors shared their ethnicity.
She pursued a PhD examining the cultural, religious and social barriers stopping Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi families from donating. She didn't stop at research. She worked directly with religious leaders and community groups, and co-founded Upahaar, a volunteer initiative that has registered over 10,000 organ and stem cell donors.
Throughout her career, she has dedicated her work to addressing inequities in healthcare and strengthening access to care. Her work has also contributed to regulatory change enabling internationally trained nurses to re-enter the UK workforce, helping address critical workforce shortages. Her contributions to patient access, community engagement and healthcare capacity have earned her recognition including the British Empire Medal.
True calling
Born and raised in the city of Kottayam, Dr Agimol knew early that nursing was her path and her decision. "I could see that I could make a large change with this career," she said.
She now plans to invest half her $250,000 prize in Upahaar and the rest in nursing education. "It's about empowering more nurses to become advocates and changemakers," she said.
She described her profession as a true calling. “The message I have for others who are considering nursing as a career is that it is a true calling,” she said. “It comes with the responsibility of being there for people when they are possibly at one of the lowest points of their lives. It requires true passion.”

title: De la sabiduría lunar al Whatsapp: la información climática que salvó las cosechas de los agricultores ecuatorianos
content:
- En Ecuador, más de 15 000 agricultores usan los boletines climáticos didácticos para planificar sus siembras y sus cosechas.
- Entre 2022 y 2025, el Instituto Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Ecuador (Inamhi) pasó de emitir 51 advertencias climáticas a 70, confirmando que los cambios en el clima van en aumento.
- La información climática permite prevenir y gestionar el riesgo de desastres y tomar mejores decisiones en agricultura para garantizar la seguridad alimentaria.
- Nuna, un chatbot, ha abierto las opciones de compartir con agricultores de la provincia de Imbabura información climática más allá de las predicciones meteorológicas.
El domingo, Evita Tupiza, la señora que tiene las vacas, la que hace el queso y lo vende el domingo en el mercado de San Blas, en la provincia de Imbabura, le dijo a Gladys Flores que el boletín meteorológico que recibe por WhatsApp la está ayudando a decidir si ordeña o no en las madrugadas. Este no es un asunto trivial para Tupiza: hacerlo bajo el sol fuerte, daña la leche y después no puede producir quesos. Saber con tiempo si va a llover o si habrá altas temperaturas, también le ayuda a prever lugares de sombra para dejar sus vacas en las mañanas.
Hasta hace diez años, quizá cinco, a Evita Tupiza le hubiese bastado con mirar a la luna. En San Blas, una parroquia rural de alrededor de 5000 personas, los agricultores se manejaban a través de “cabañuelas”, cálculos ancestrales en que, observando las variaciones atmosféricas de los primeros días del mes de enero, podían pronosticar el tiempo de los próximos doce meses. Los que sabían leer, acudirían al almanaque Bristol, ese famoso folleto naranja con el doctor Cyrenius Charles Bristol en la portada llevando un traje de hace casi dos siglos. Esta revista que se imprime ininterrumpidamente desde 1832, trae predicciones astronómicas, astrológicas, el calendario lunar y consejos para la siembra
Sin embargo, ahora ni las cabañuelas, ni el almanaque, ni la luna aciertan en sus predicciones del clima, según manifiestan con desconcierto los agricultores de San Blas.
Leer más |Santa Martha: una comunidad cacataibo de Perú cercada por el narcotráfico y el recorte territorial
Como Gaby Flores y Evita Tupiza, alrededor de 15 000 agricultores en Ecuador ―según un informe del Programa Mundial de Alimentos― han mejorado, potenciado o salvado sus cosechas, su tierra y sus animales, gracias a los boletines meteorológicos que líderes comunitarios, servidores públicos de las prefecturas y comuneros capacitados, comparten en los grupos de WhatsApp.
Como una especie de guardianes del clima, estas personas masifican informes que, de manera digerible, explican los datos que el Instituto Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Ecuador (Inamhi) produce en tiempo real. Esto es un asunto vital para los ecuatorianos ya que en los últimos cinco años los eventos climáticos extremos han ido en aumento. Entre 2022 y 2025, el Inamhi pasó de emitir 51 advertencias climáticas a 70.
Información y buenas decisiones
La frontera de Ecuador y Colombia fue el punto de partida de un proyecto ambicioso de adaptación climática incentivado por el Programa Mundial de Alimentos (WFP por sus siglas en inglés) en coordinación con gobiernos locales y otras instituciones públicas. Inició en 2018 con el objetivo de fortalecer las capacidades adaptativas alrededor de las dos cuencas hidrográficas que cruzan y unen los dos países, la Mira-Mataje y la Guáitara-Carchi.
Estas zonas incluyen dos departamentos colombianos y cuatro provincias ecuatorianas con población mayoritariamente indígena y afrodescendiente asentadas en cinco ecosistemas frágiles: manglares, bosques secos, bosques tropicales húmedos, bosques nublados y matorrales; que ya venían sufriendo las variabilidades climáticas del calentamiento global.
Durante seis años se realizaron decenas de colaboraciones estratégicas. Formación a líderes comunitarios, especialmente mujeres, en procesos participativos de 97 comunidades afrodescendientes y 76 comunidades indígenas Awá. Se instalaron 30 equipos meteorológicos, se coordinaron encuentros binacionales, se realizaron rescates de saberes ancestrales, se documentaron más de 350 especies de plantas nativas o tradicionales con atributos nutricionales y nueve boletines climáticos comenzaron a circular entre las 24 000 personas que participaron en las capacitaciones sobre cambio climático. Pasaron una pandemia, el aumento de la violencia en Ecuador, la presencia de grupos armados en la frontera con Colombia y, sin embargo, desde 2024 se comenzaron a ver los frutos que parten de un empoderamiento social de los datos científicos.
“Si tú no tienes información, no vas a poder tomar buenas decisiones, vas a estar corriendo en círculos porque no sabes a qué te estás enfrentando, a qué amenaza y en qué nivel de exposición estás”, dice Diego Guzmán, oficial de cambio climático y sistemas agroalimentarios de WPF. La idea aplica a varios aspectos de la vida, pero Guzmán se refiere a los factores climáticos que perturban, en mayor medida, a comunidades no preparadas para asumir los nuevos escenarios ecológicos.
Esto lo corroboran dos técnicos sentados en una oficina austera de muros cremas del segundo piso del edificio de la prefectura de Imbabura.
Edison Marcial y Vinicio Fuentes asistieron a varias de las capacitaciones de sistemas de manejo de datos meteorológicos que dictaron especialistas del Inamhi. Les explicaron lo más complicado y teórico de los procesos científicos de la meteorología: qué satélites se usan, cómo hacen las agencias nacionales los pronósticos del tiempo, qué son los modelos matemáticos de predicción, las plataformas digitales en las que se procesan los datos, los mapas de color y el monitoreo en tiempo real en el Visor Hidrometeorológico Nacional.
“Es de acceso público toda la información”, dice Edison Marcial, mientras muestra una imagen en su teléfono celular: un mapa de la provincia de Imbabura con unos aros de colores, en la gama del verde al rojo. “El Inamhi te manda así, la imagen en bruto”.
El WPF hizo que personal del propio Inamhi capacitara a dos funcionarios de cada provincia en Ecuador y departamento en Colombia. El objetivo era que los técnicos locales entendieran los modelos de predicción oficiales y los tradujeran de tal manera que cualquier persona los pudiera interpretar. Fue así que la primera parte del proyecto de creación de boletines climáticos, en 2024, dio como resultado nueve boletines (entre semanales y diarios) que llegaron a compartirse entre 15 000 agricultores de los dos países.
Los primeros boletines salvaron las cosechas
En 2024, Ecuador rompió los récord de temperaturas altas con sequías extremas: más de 80 000 hectáreas quemadas y una grave crisis energética, según datos de la Secretaría Nacional de Riesgos. Ese mismo año, los boletines meteorológicos didácticos comenzaron a circular cada tres días, en las provincias de Carchi, Imbabura, Esmeraldas y Sucumbíos. Se trataba de una imagen con el mapa de la provincia y la intensidad de las lluvias. Una leyenda de seis colores que variaba desde el rojo (que significa lluvias intensas) y el verde en el medio (señal de lluvia moderada), hasta llegar al blanco que indica ausencia total de lluvia. A un costado se mostraban las temperaturas máximas y mínimas.
Esto evitó pérdidas en la zona del Valle del Chota y en la zona de Urcuquí, en la Provincia de Imbabura, donde está el terreno familiar de Gladys Flores, hija, nieta y bisnieta de campesinos.
“Cuando era pequeña, mi bisabuela me contaba que sus padres también fueron agricultores en este mismo terreno”, dice Flores mientras recorre sus sembríos, mostrándolos con orgullo. Es la quinta generación que trabaja esa tierra.
En su casa de ladrillos, madera y techo de Eternit, ella y su esposo, César Vinueza, comparten una limonada y sus experiencias en el campo. Cuentan que el agua que riega sus productos es muy limpia porque viene cinco kilómetros arriba del río Warmiyaku, dónde está la captación.
“Esa piscina de captación y la acequia [canal artificial a cielo abierto] es de antes de la venida de los españoles. Es muy antigua”, comenta Flores.“Mi papá sabía con exactitud cuándo venía el verano y la época seca. Ahora llueve cuando no es de llover. Encima, el caudal del río ha bajado bastante. Antes no podíamos controlar la fuerza del agua cuando nos tocaba el turno del riego. Ahora baja poquito. Toca estar yendo a ver qué pasa en la captación y que todo esté bien”.
Leer más | Día Internacional de los Primates: tres proyectos para salvarlos del tráfico y la pérdida de hábitat
Con menos agua de riego y más sequía, Flores, su esposo y todo el pueblo de San Blas están “cosechando agua”, es decir, llenan unos tanques enormes de plástico que recuperan el agua cuando llueve.
“En 2024 vino fuerte la sequía. Nos tocó hacer turnos con las demás compañeras. Cada 15 días recibimos el agua de la acequia para regar nuestros terrenos. Justo en ese tiempo llegaron los boletines y, viendo en las fotos que iba a estar seca la época que normalmente era de lluvia, atrasamos el cultivo del fréjol. Gracias a esas cartillas no perdimos tanto de nuestro trabajo”, recuerda Gladys Flores.
César Vinueza, el esposo de Gladys, cuenta que la casa en la que viven fue construida para un lugar frío, cerca a los páramos que es donde se asienta San Blas. Sin embargo, el calor actual es tan fuerte que el techo que tenía que guardar el calor, ahora lo acumula de tal manera que tienen que hacer ciertos cambios. “Estoy preocupado, nunca me imaginé que el Eternit fuera tan caliente. A la una de la tarde es insoportable, por eso voy a arreglar esas dos ventanas para que entre el aire directo, como casa de la costa”.
Todos ríen.
Flores y Vinueza se juntaron con otras mujeres agricultoras para crear la asociación agropecuaria “Frutos de mi Tierra”. Casi llegan a los 10 años llevando sus productos a la feria del pueblo los domingos y los miércoles en la Universidad Yachay.
Leer más | Eric Terena, el DJ indígena que denuncia el silenciamiento de la Amazonía | ENTREVISTA
“Nuestro principal orgullo es que hemos eliminado a los intermediarios, de aquí salen los productos directo a los compradores”, dice Vinueza.
Gladys Flores administra el grupo de WhatsApp de la asociación y es la encargada de compartir, cada tres días, el boletín climático que la prefectura de Imbabura le envía a ella.
Desde que se dieron cuenta que con esa información pudieron evitar una siembra de fréjol que se perdería por la sequía inesperada de 2024, las mujeres de Frutos de mi Tierra son acérrimas usuarias del boletín que, en dos años, tuvo una cadena de innovaciones que superó las expectativas de los propios organismos estatales y de cooperación internacional que iniciaron el proyecto en 2018.
Flores cuenta que gracias a los videos que reciben con los pronósticos y las alertas climáticas, las mujeres campesinas que no saben leer y escribir ya no tienen que mostrar la infografía colorida a sus hijos o nietos para que confirmen lo que ellas ven en colores, sino que con el audio ya “entienden todito”. Y que esa información, como le dijo Evita Tupiza, le ha permitido planificar el ordeño de sus vacas para la producción de los quesos.
El aficionado al arte que prepara a los agricultores
Vinicio Fuentes es agrónomo y tiene un máster en sistemas de información geográfica, pero habla como productor de televisión o creador de contenidos.
Sentado frente a su computadora, busca emocionado los primeros videos que creó a partir de los pronósticos oficiales del Inamhi. Fuentes no se conformó con mandar el boletín de colores y fue más allá. Primero, le puso voz y animó la imagen. De inmediato se dio cuenta que los agricultores comenzaron a estar pendientes de la información.
“Lo que siempre estoy pensando es: ¿cómo hago digeribles todos estos datos? Por suerte han tenido la paciencia de permitirme la prueba y el error”, cuenta Fuentes con una sonrisa disimulada que muestra cómo disfruta de su trabajo.
Uno de los problemas más frecuentes que enfrentó en sus procesos de comunicación era que la persona que hacía las locuciones no estaba siempre disponible para cuando el boletín climático comenzó a ser un ritual. Entonces Fuentes probó con una voz de inteligencia artificial. Esto fue un éxito porque le permitió hacer más eficiente la producción de los boletines cada tres días. Con el tiempo, y con las pruebas, también se dio cuenta que los videos debían ser más cortos para que no fueran “tan pesados” y los usuarios pudieran abrirlos desde sus teléfonos.
“Lo que la gente necesita saber es si va a llover o no”, dice con la seguridad de la experiencia, Edison Marcial, quien fue parte del Programa Mundial de Alimentos antes de trabajar en la prefectura de Imbabura. Asegura ser testigo de cómo el interés de Vinicio Fuentes y sus ganas de mejorar los boletines hicieron que Imbabura fuera pionera de iniciativas mucho más ambiciosas como “Nuna”, el chatbot, o la Granja Digital, una plataforma con datos públicos y accesibles con los cuales los productores de Imbabura pueden consultar información sobre sus predios, la fertilidad de sus suelos y buenas prácticas agrícolas.
“Vimos que WhatsApp es uno de los medios masivos de comunicación entre las comunidades agrícolas”, comenta Fuentes mientras conecta su computadora a una pantalla gigante en la oficina de uno de sus jefes para mostrar cómo funciona el chatbot que creó.
Con un grupo de creativos dieron vida a un personaje que suma todas las características culturales de los diferentes pueblos de Imbabura. Se llama Nuna y significa “alma” o “energía vital” en kichwa. Tiene la máscara tradicional de diablo huma pero con plumas de los colibríes que existen en los diferentes cantones de la provincia.
“La idea fue tener un chat en el que puedes hacer consultas continuamente y ya no ser un usuario pasivo que recibe los boletines”, dice Fuentes con orgullo.
En la pantalla se abre la conversación. ¡Hola, soy Nuna, tu asistente virtual de la Prefectura de Imbabura, gracias por tu mensaje! Nuna abre una serie de opciones: Geoparque Imbabura, Clima, Ferias Productoras, Rutas Turísticas, Novedades, Smartfarm y Servicios Mecánicos.
“Aprovechamos que tenemos toda esta lógica de comunicación a partir del boletín climático, que fue el inicio de esto, para potenciar y difundir toda la información que tenemos como Prefectura”, explica Fuentes.
Al dar click a la opción “Clima”, Nuna comparte el video del boletín agroclimático de Imbabura, las advertencias meteorológicas nacionales del Inamhi (información adicional sobre eventos intensos de lluvias o sequías) y el calendario lunar, como una forma de incluir y respetar la diversidad cultural.
Desde el 1 de enero al 31 de mayo de 2026, el Inamhi había registrado 2026 eventos adversos como inundaciones, deslizamientos y aluviones.
Leer más | Antártida: cierran la pesquería de kril por sobrepesca y crece la alerta por sus impactos
El aprendizaje se aprovecha y se comparte en cadena
Esta nueva forma de entregar información climática está llegando a todo el país. El 4 de junio de 2026, PWF, Inamhi, Ministerio de Ambiente y Energía y representantes de las prefecturas de Imbabura y Manabí ―provincia ecuatoriana costera que sufre inundaciones continuas― se reunieron en la Capilla del Hombre, en Quito. Era el lanzamiento oficial de los boletines nacionales del Inamhi. “De la información climática a la acción territorial” se llamó el evento
Vinicio Fuentes, muy tímido, parado al fondo de la sala con los brazos echados para atrás, escuchaba las intervenciones de las autoridades, de los científicos y el testimonio de Juan De Mera Centeno, agricultor de la asociación Raíces Manabas que produce principalmente arroz, verduras, hortalizas y frutas en Manabí. “Al tener acceso a esta información optimizamos tiempo y recursos. Por ejemplo, para el trasplante de una semilla, si sabemos que va a llover, ponemos en pausa el trabajo porque inundado el suelo, todo se pierde”, dice el campesino de la costa ecuatoriana.
Manabí es la segunda provincia que hace los boletines meteorológicos con video para alrededor de 9000 agricultores.
“No fue fácil motivar a la prefectura de Manabí para que haga los boletines metereológicos”, confiesa Diego Guzmán de PWF. “Allá no creen, o no creían―Guzmán suelta una risa― en la cooperación internacional”.
Fue entonces cuando invitaron a Vinicio Fuentes a la Prefectura de la provincia costera. Él contó su experiencia a Jairo Moreira, su par, el encargado de compartir la información que recibe del Inamhi a las diferentes organizaciones de agricultores de Manabí.
“El PWF nos dio el equipamiento, un ordenador con un programa de edición de video. El Inamhi nos capacitó para interpretar los datos y los mapas que nos envían. El ingeniero Vinicio nos enseñó cómo ellos hacen los videos con palabras más sencillas. Así iniciamos la producción de los boletines aquí”, confirma Moreira.
Y pasó algo que no esperaba: los usuarios de Manabí tampoco se pierden un solo boletín. Al igual que en Imbabura, el video corto y didáctico ha hecho que sus agricultores usen esta información como parte de su trabajo. A partir de los boletines toman decisiones sobre sus tierras y sus productos.
Por ejemplo, si ven que va a llover, los productores de cacao no sacan a secar sus semillas. También les ayuda a planificar la época de siembra y de cosecha de productos de ciclo corto.
“Esto lo implementamos en diciembre de 2024 y el testimonio de los agricultores es que, con esta información hacen mucho mejor su trabajo porque pueden adaptarse a las variaciones climáticas”, dice Moreira y agrega que cuando se demoran y no envían el boletín a tiempo, los campesinos usuarios los llaman, los presionan y les preguntan qué pasó con el boletín. “Ha tenido muy buena aceptación. Ahora nos lo piden asociaciones que están fuera de los grupos de la Prefectura. También estudiantes de universidades y otras federaciones de campesinos”.
Ese 4 de junio en La Capilla del Hombre, uno de los complejos arquitectónicos y culturales más importantes de Quito, Matteo Perrone, representante de PWF para Ecuador, dijo a una sala llena que uno de los principales logros del proyecto de adaptación al cambio climático en Ecuador fue la descentralización del conocimiento.
Luego, pasaron un video hecho por los técnicos del Inhami. Tomando la idea de la prefectura de Imbabura, ahora los boletines nacionales también se harán en video con una voz en IA que cuenta lo que significan los colores en el mapa de calor.
Pocos entre la gente del evento saben que el hombre que está de pie al otro lado del escenario, con las manos echadas para atrás, que le gusta tocar guitarra, piano y editar los boletines climáticos en CapCut, es Vinicio Fuentes, quien, con su motivación, logró que se replique la forma de informar y dar herramientas a los agricultores que él inició hace algún tiempo desde Imbabura.

title: Founding father Tan Cheng Lock’s pantun diplomacy won hearts
content:
Tan Siok Choo, 73, said notwithstanding Cheng Lock’s gift for oratory, the man widely recognised as one of the founding fathers of Malaysia also cemented his standing as a local leader through his strong Melaka Peranakan roots.
She said he established himself as a captain of industry who championed the community’s needs.
“He did not start a populist mass movement or anything like that. But he was well known, particularly in Melaka and Singapore.
“He was a very good public speaker, very good at communicating, issuing statements and so forth. I think what helped was the fact that he was a sixth-generation Peranakan living in Melaka,” she told FMT in a recent interview.
Siok Choo was speaking to FMT after the recent launch of the biography “One Country, One People: The Life and Legacy of Tun Tan Cheng Lock”, which she edited with academic Heng Pek Koon.
She noted that her grandfather was a pioneer in the rubber business, having founded United Malacca Bhd in 1910, which is one of the country’s oldest rubber plantation companies listed on Bursa Malaysia.
While Cheng Lock built a reputation as an industrialist, his later involvement in banking, including as a founding director of the Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation in 1932, made him even better known in the community.
“He was on the board of the bank for 30 years. I think that gave him visibility, as people know you always go to a bank for help. People started getting to know him as someone who could help,” she said.
Siok Choo said the Chinese community also identified with Cheng Lock’s strong Confucian beliefs, exemplified by the woodwork and paintings in his ancestral home.
She pointed out that in front of the house’s hall of filial remembrance, where the family’s ancestors are venerated, there are carvings depicting stories from the Three Kingdoms and paintings of figures from Confucian teachings.
“Those who are familiar with Chinese culture can relate to it. It is an ancestral home thoroughly infused with Confucian ideals and philosophy.
“You can relate to the fact that this house belonged to a guy who couldn’t read (Chinese), but surrounded himself with Chinese literature and philosophy,” she said.
Cheng Lock was not only held in high esteem among the Chinese but he also had no difficulty building bridges with the Malays, mainly because of his Peranakan roots.
“One of his habits that endeared him to the Malays was that he loved reciting Malay pantun at the drop of a hat. And he was actually quite good at the language because he would adapt pantun for particular purposes,” said Siok Choo.
The biography notes the first meeting between Cheng Lock and Umno founder Onn Jaafar in Johor Bahru on Dec 29, 1948, during which a Malay leader praised Cheng Lock for his ability to recite pantun.
Cheng Lock was also described by former prime minister Tunku Abdul Rahman as “one of Malaya’s illustrious sons”, prompted by his repeated calls for all who considered the country their home to regard themselves as Malayans first, regardless of race.

title: Museum agrees to return remains to ancestral homeland
content:
Museum agrees to return remains to ancestral homeland
- Published
More than three dozen sets of human remains taken during the British colonial rule of India and Myanmar are set to be returned to their ancestral home by a museum.
Skulls and bones belonging to the Naga people of northeastern India and Myanmar - formerly known as Burma - have been displayed at the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford for more than a century.
In 2020, the museum removed all human remains from public display as part of what the it called a "decolonisation process" - including the ancestral Naga remains.
The museum has now announced that a formal decision has been made by the University of Oxford Council to return the 39 ancestral human remains to their homeland.
"They've been here in a foreign land for more than a century," Dr Vihuto Asumi, President of the Sumî Hoho Naga tribe, said of the remains.
"We believe that their spirits are still not at rest - so by doing this, we believe it will bring spiritual healing, not only to the ancestral remains here but to everyone who died during the head-hunting days."
The Pitt Rivers claims to hold the largest collection of Naga artefacts in the world, most of which were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar.
Many were acquired by John Henry Hutton, a colonial administrator in the Indian Civil Service and an anthropologist, who handed them to the museum more than a century ago.
Among the museum's Naga collection - which contains several thousand items - are 219 items listed as human remains, 39 ancestral human remains and 178 objects that are thought to contain human hair.
The latest announcement concerns only the ancestral remains, and follows a declaration made by a Naga delegation visiting Oxford in 2025, in which the group requested the objects be returned.
The museum's director, Prof Laura Van Broekhoven, said: "It has been a long journey to get to this moment."
"We know that this week will be one where we will feel both grief and sadness when looking back on that past, and also where hope is possible as we work towards reconciliation and healing."
Following the decision, the Pitt Rivers is now organising an official handover ceremony involving a Naga delegation.
The Naga will then accompany the remains of their ancestors home, with some returning for the first time in more than a century.

title: The God who lived in our conscience
content:
The house is humming. The family is gathering. The old toys are coming out.
And Papa is about to build a universe.
Janmashtami in our home was never simply a festival we observed. It was a world we assembled.
Every year, Papa—my father, Deepak—would help us build the jhanki. From trunks and cupboards came old toys, some handed down from my grandparents’ generation, their paint faded, their limbs occasionally loose, their faces carrying the strange solemnity of objects that had survived more childhoods than one.
Little cows. Little cowherds. Little people. Little gods.
Krishna. Radha. The gopis. Animals. Deities.
An entire civilisation waiting patiently in boxes for someone to bring it back to life.
And for a few enchanted days every Janmashtami, that someone was us.
My brother Samir and I, my sister Seema, and our cousins Sumita, Sangeeta and Raghav gathered around the grown-ups with the seriousness children reserve for projects adults mistakenly imagine are merely play.
Our Bhua, Deepa, was there. Her husband, our Phuphaji, Hargobind Bhatnagar. Our mother, Sunita. Papa, Deepak.
And above all, in the great constellation of my childhood memory, there was Dadi, Kamla Bhatnagar.
Her husband, my paternal grandfather, Bade Papaji, was Bhagat Saran Bhatnagar. They belonged to that generation that seemed to carry libraries in their memories and histories in their habits.
But Dadi did something remarkable.
She told us mythology without demanding that we surrender our minds.
Who knew a grandmother could be so cool?
She did not tell us these stories as if curiosity were a sin. She taught us to wonder, to question, to listen, to imagine.
Mythology, she seemed to suggest, was not the enemy of science. Science was not the assassin of mythology.
Both were humanity’s attempts to understand what it could see and what it could not.
Sometimes mythology reached towards a truth before science had found the language to explain it. Sometimes
science arrived centuries later and illuminated what mythology had been trying to imagine.
Sometimes they disagreed.
Sometimes they danced.
And sometimes they simply stood across the room from one another, equally aware that humanity still knew very
little about the mystery of being alive.
For us, however, the mystery of Janmashtami began with atta.
The Yamuna flowed through our jhanki, made from kneaded flour.
We shaped riverbanks and bends with our hands. We painted them with watercolours—blue for the river, brown for the earth, green for the trees.
Give a child flour and water, and he will make geography.
Give him an old toy, and he will make history.
Give him a shoebox and a mirror, and he will make the weather.
Papa, Samir and I did exactly that.
The greatest thrill of Janmashtami for me was our sound-and-light drama. We took a shoebox and turned it into a primitive projector. We found mirrors, reflective glass, coloured cellophane, scraps of plastic, anything that could catch or bend light.
Blue became night.
Silver became lightning.
Grey became rain.
Darkness became danger.
Light became revelation.
We created monsoon storms with mirrors and scraps.

And somewhere in the middle of all that glorious amateur theatre, Papa would begin the commentary.
Then Dadi would add something.
Bhua would remember another version.
Phuphaji would interrupt.
Someone would correct someone else.
Someone would laugh.
And the story of Krishna would rise from the floor, the walls and the flickering light.
We were not reading mythology.
We were staging it.
There was Kansa—evil, frightened, furious Kansa, haunted by the prophecy that a child would one day bring about his end.
There was the prison.
Devaki.
Vasudeva.
The newborn Krishna.
A child whose first breath was taken in captivity.
And then came the great crossing.
Vasudeva carrying the baby in a tokri.
The storm.

The river.
The danger.
The darkness.
The desperate journey towards safety.

title: The diamond jubilee of India’s green shield: Indian Forest Service completes 60 years
content:
The diamond jubilee of India’s green shield: Indian Forest Service completes 60 years
Corbett transitioned from a hunter of man-eaters to a wildlife champion, helping establish India's first National Park in 1936.
At the borders of Kuno National Park where India's famous Project Cheetah is underway, high-tech conservation meets human survival. Solar smart fences, thermal cameras, and satellites guard one side, while villages pressure nature on the other. This juxtaposition defines the frontline of the Indian Forest Service, which recently marked six decades since its modern inception on 1 July 1966.
The roots of the Service trace back to 1864, when Germany's Sir Dietrich Brandis became India's first Inspector General of Forests, replacing chaotic jungle exploitation with scientific forestry. Later, legendary figures like Jim Corbett gave the Service its soul, shifting forestry from timber production to habitat protection. Corbett transitioned from a hunter of man-eaters to a wildlife champion, helping establish India's first National Park in 1936. This trajectory led to the 1966 constitutional formalisation of the modern Indian Forest Service as an elite All India Service (AIS) dedicated to ecological governance, mitigating climate change, and halting habitat loss.
Also Read | Posting IFS officers as rural development project directors will paralyse public services: PMK
Global Standing and Mindset Shift
India holds 2.2% of global land while supporting 18% of the human population and heavy livestock pressures. Despite this, structured conservation has placed India among the world's top ten forest-rich nations. According to the FAO’s Global Forest Resource Assessment, India ranks 9th globally in total forest area and 3rd for net annual forest cover gains, with its canopy covering 25.17% of the landmass.This expanding canopy supports India's target of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2070. To meet this, the nation plans to sequester an additional 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes (GT) of CO2 equivalents through enhanced green cover by 2030. Alongside carbon sink expansion, India has rapidly expanded its network of Ramsar sites, vastly upgrading vital wetland protections.
This growth required a major policy shift. While the 1952 National Forest Policy treated woods as commercial assets, the 1988 policy subordinated industrial profits to ecological balance. This shift birthed Joint Forest Management (JFM) in 1990, giving communities a share of forest benefits and steadily replacing the traditional paradigm of bitter human-wildlife conflict with a sustainable ethos of human-wildlife coexistence.Legal and Modern PillarsThe green governance relies on a powerful legal architecture anchored by the historical Indian Forest Act (IFA) of 1927, which provides vital enforcement teeth for field staff.
Over decades, it has transitioned to work alongside a modern quartet of laws evolved by the Service: the Wildlife Protection Act, the Forest Conservation Act (FCA) 1980—renamed the Van Sanrakshan evam Samwardhan Adhiniyam in 2023—the Biological Diversity Act, and the Forest Rights Act (FRA). The 1980 legislation sharply reduced unchecked wilderness conversion. Today, developers pay the net present value of diversions into the CAMPA fund for large-scale afforestation.
Legal protection strengthened further with the landmark T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad (1996) case, where the Supreme Court expanded jurisdiction to all lands matching the dictionary definition of a "forest," making the Service the sole custodian of green cover. Down at the community level, the FRA of 2006 recognized traditional dwellers' rights, reducing distress migration and securing local livelihoods.
On the ground, the National Working Plan Code has evolved from counting logs into a scientific blueprint tracking carbon capture and watershed health. Young officers entering the Indira Gandhi National Forest Academy (IGNFA) frequently hold advanced degrees in engineering, medicine, and data analytics. They oversee a frontline equipped with the M-STrIPES platform, a digital net connecting handheld patrol modules with a central GIS analytical engine. This accountability has scaled up Project Tiger (58 Tiger Reserves) and Project Elephant (33 Reserves), helping India host an estimated 3,682 wild tigers and 22,446 wild elephants.
Also Read | Ecological equity needs constitutional protection
The Frontline Reality
However, technology cannot execute an arrest. Humans must still march into pitch-black jungles to face armed timber syndicates, poachers, and sand mafias. This danger continues to extract a heavy cost; over sixty years, hundreds of forest personnel, including officers, have died in the line of duty. The Service honours the historic martyrdom of heroes like Kirti Chakra P. Srinivas, killed by the smuggler Veerappan, and Sanjay Singh, who made the supreme sacrifice fighting mining mafias.
Today's green guards also face climate-driven forest fires, urbanization challenges, and invasive weeds choking grasslands. Yet, by leveraging smart technologies and local partnerships, the frontline continues to actively foster human-wildlife coexistence in rapidly changing landscapes. Inspiringly, this frontline is getting increasingly inclusive, with women making up nearly 20 percent of the incoming batches of officer trainees. The journey of the Service proves a determined nation can prioritize growth without compromising on its wilderness.
As the renowned author Ruskin Bond told Indian Foresters:
"Without your help to Nature's thrust,
This land would be a bowl of dust."
Our future livability rests on the shoulders of these guards celebrating the completion of 60 years of the green frame. In ensuring that our forests breathe, they ensure that India thrives. Their silent sentinel remains the ultimate shield for our collective tomorrow.
(Raj Kumar Bajpai is an Additional Director with the Indian Forest Services 1994 Batch, Jharkhand Cadre).

title: Em território retomado no morro Santana, ‘Gaton – A Força da Terra’ reforça a luta kaingang pelo direito à terra
content:
No domingo (13), a Aldeia Gah Re, localizada no morro Santana, zona leste de Porto Alegre, recebeu o segundo encontro do lançamento do livro “Gaton – A Força da Terra”. A obra reúne histórias, memórias e saberes do povo kaingang e tem como autora a jovem escritora Kapri Audisséia Nascimento Padilha. Sua principal fonte de narrativas é sua mãe, a cacica Iracema Gãh Té Nascimento, liderança política e espiritual da aldeia.
A publicação nasce de um processo coletivo envolvendo mãe e filha, junto das antropólogas Ana Letícia Meira Schweig (edição e projeto gráfico) e Geórgia Macedo (produção cultural e escrita). Em reuniões e conversas, Kapri e Iracema foram selecionando produções, lembrando trajetórias e definindo quais assuntos eram importantes para compor o livro.
Os netos da cacica acompanharam de perto todo o processo. Enquanto ouviam os relatos dos mais velhos, as crianças refletiam sobre como traduzi-los visualmente. Essas ideias foram transformadas em ilustrações durante oficinas de desenho conduzidas por Ana Letícia, passando a integrar as páginas da obra.
O trabalho uniu a transmissão oral e a participação infantil de forma contínua: à medida que as memórias emergiam, as crianças as assimilavam e planejavam a arte da publicação, fortalecendo os laços comunitários e a preservação da cultura Kaingang.
“Botar no papel os saberes kaingang”
Para Kapri, o livro concretiza um sonho antigo da mãe: registrar os saberes kaingang para que sejam transmitidos de geração em geração.
O lançamento na Aldeia Gah Re reforça o caráter político da obra. A comunidade kaingang Gah Re, que retomou o território do morro Santana em 2022, espera que o livro alcance Brasília e contribua no debate no Poder Judiciário sobre a importância do território indígena. “A gente espera, a Comunidade Indígena kaingang Gah Re, que isso ecoa até o pessoal que está lá em Brasília, que está no Poder Judiciário sobre a importância do território indígena”, diz Kapri
A obra não é a primeira colaboração da Geórgia Macedo com a Gãh Teh. A antropóloga conta que sua trajetória na produção cultural se alinha ao desejo da cacica, que já vinha comentando que gostaria de produzir um livro. “Eu trabalho há muitos anos já com a Gãh Teh, com os povos indígenas, mas acho que comecei, entrei nessa caminhada junto com a Gãh Teh. Já atuo há muitos anos na produção cultural, no cinema, na dança, no teatro. Porém, é a primeira vez que estou produzindo um livro junto com elas”, relata.
Macedo foi a responsável pelos aspectos burocráticos do processo. “Desde que a gente escreveu o livro, elas já estavam na frente. Eu estava sempre como uma mediadora dessas relações com o Estado, essas relações burocráticas. É um edital público, então tem muitas questões de entrega de documentos, prazos, prestação de contas, tanto do objeto como financeira”, explica.
“Muitos filhos da Terra se perderam”
Questionada sobre o que a motivou a colocar suas histórias e saberes no livro, a cacica Iracema aponta uma preocupação espiritual e com as novas gerações. “Estou vendo muitos filhos da Terra se perderem, como a gente acredita muito e tem a fé espiritual, quem sabe pessoas lendo vão pensar ou meditar”, afirma a cacica.
O próximo lançamento será nesta quarta-feira (16), das 14h às 16h, no Instituto de Filosofia e Ciências Humanas (IFCH/UFRGS), mediação da antropóloga Geórgia Macedo.

title: No More Speeches, Pres Ali: Put Guyana’s Indigenous Wealth in Indigenous Hands
content:
As Guyana commemorates Amerindian Heritage Month, the nation must pause and reflect honestly on the condition, aspirations and future of its First Peoples. Last evening, I listened carefully to the address delivered by President Irfaan Ali at Whirl Wind Village, Sophia. While speeches and expressions of appreciation for Indigenous peoples are important, our First Peoples deserve far more than ceremonial words. They deserve meaningful action, economic empowerment, ownership and opportunities capable of transforming their communities for generations to come.
Amerindian Heritage Month should not be reduced to a period when politicians visit Indigenous communities, deliver speeches, celebrate their culture and make promises. It must be a time when the country asks a fundamental question: What tangible economic opportunities are being created to place Indigenous people in control of their own future?
One area where the Government of Guyana can make a significant difference is Indigenous tourism ownership. Guyana possesses extraordinary natural beauty, wildlife, rivers, forests and Indigenous cultures with enormous potential for sustainable tourism. Yet too often, the greatest economic benefits from tourism flow to businesses and investors from outside the communities where these attractions are located. That approach must change.
The Government should establish an Indigenous Tourism Ownership Programme designed in consultation with Indigenous leaders, village councils, communities and other stakeholders. The objective should be straightforward: Indigenous communities should not merely participate in tourism; they should own it.
Under such a programme, the Government could provide initial capital financing, technical assistance, training and business support, while the Indigenous village or community retains ownership of the enterprise. The programme could support village-owned eco-lodges and guest houses, tour boats and river excursions, birdwatching and wildlife businesses, Indigenous craft and cultural shops, fishing and angling tours, jungle and forest excursions, cultural and heritage experiences, traditional food and culinary tourism, and nature tours, community transportation services, camping and adventure-tourism facilities, as well as traditional arts, music and cultural performances.
These would only be starting points. The communities themselves should determine which businesses are appropriate for their environment, culture and aspirations. Nobody in Georgetown should be deciding from an office what an Indigenous community needs or what kind of enterprise can succeed in that community.
This is the fundamental change Guyana needs. Our Indigenous brothers and sisters should not always be treated as beneficiaries of Government programmes. They should be owners, entrepreneurs, employers and investors in their own communities.
Imagine a village owning an eco-lodge where visitors stay. The village owns the property and the boats. The village employs the tour guides, produces and sells its crafts, provides the food and conducts the cultural tours. The village earns the revenue, and that revenue is reinvested into education, healthcare, infrastructure, youth programmes and further economic development. That is what empowerment should mean.
The Government has an important role to play, but Government assistance must not become Government ownership. Initial capital could come through a dedicated Indigenous Tourism Development Fund, providing grants or low-interest financing for viable community-owned projects. However, the Indigenous community must retain ownership and have a meaningful say in how the enterprise is managed.
Such a programme would require proper governance, transparent accounting, professional training and business development support. Indigenous entrepreneurs should receive training in hospitality, accounting, marketing, digital commerce, tour management, environmental conservation and customer service. The Government can also assist communities in accessing international tourism markets and developing partnerships with airlines, hotels, travel agencies and online booking platforms. But the Indigenous community must remain at the centre of the enterprise.
Any serious Indigenous development programme must be designed with Indigenous communities, not merely for them. The Government must sit down with village councils, Indigenous leaders, young people, women, entrepreneurs, traditional leaders and community members and ask what they want for their communities, what businesses they believe can succeed, what resources they already possess, what support they need and how their culture and traditions can be protected while creating economic opportunities.
Development cannot be imposed from Georgetown. It must be built in partnership with the communities themselves. The people who live in these communities understand their land, rivers, forests, traditions and challenges better than any consultant or politician.
There is also another issue that must be confronted honestly. Our Indigenous people must not become political decorations. Every political party should respect the fact that our First Peoples are citizens of Guyana whose dignity, livelihoods, culture, land, education and economic future must be placed above partisan politics.
Indigenous communities should not only be remembered during elections, political rallies or Heritage Month celebrations. They deserve attention every day of the year. Guyana must move beyond the politics of photographs, speeches and promises. Our Indigenous people deserve measurable results. They deserve businesses, jobs, modern infrastructure, quality education, healthcare, reliable transportation and connectivity. They deserve opportunities for their young people to remain in their communities because they can build prosperous lives there. Above all, they deserve ownership and dignity.
The Government of Guyana has an opportunity to demonstrate that Amerindian Heritage Month can become more than a month of speeches. Let it become the beginning of a new national policy of Indigenous economic ownership. Let the country establish community-owned tourism enterprises, put capital into the hands of Indigenous communities, train Indigenous entrepreneurs, create opportunities for Indigenous youth, strengthen village economies and protect Indigenous culture and the environment while creating sustainable income.
When tourists travel into Guyana’s hinterland, the Indigenous communities whose lands, rivers, forests and cultures make the experience possible must be among the principal owners and beneficiaries of that tourism economy. It is not enough for outsiders to profit while the communities receive occasional employment, small contracts or ceremonial recognition.
President Irfaan Ali and the PPP Government have an opportunity to move from words to action. Amerindian Heritage Month should not end with another speech. It should begin with a programme, a budget, a timeline and measurable results.
Our First Peoples have contributed to the story of Guyana since long before the modern State existed. Their culture, knowledge, traditions and relationship with the land are an indispensable part of our national identity. We must therefore ensure that their future is not determined by dependency, political promises or outside ownership.
Let Guyana build Indigenous communities that own, operate and benefit from the economic opportunities within their own homeland. Let the country stop repeatedly failing its First Peoples. Let their livelihoods, culture, dignity and future be paramount.
Amerindian Heritage Month must be about more than remembering our First Peoples. It must be about empowering them and not to subject them.
Pt.Ubraj Narine, JP, COA
Former Staff Sgt.(GDF), Mayor
City of Georgetown

title: Ramaphosa lists and praises SA’s heritage traits
content:
Story audio is generated using AI
“Heritage is more than just a celebration of the past, it is the knowledge, traditions and values South Africans pass from one generation to the next,” said President Cyril Ramaphosa during a National Heritage Day celebration keynote address at Bongolethu Sports Stadium in Oudtshoorn, Western Cape, on Thursday.
Ramaphosa said the country’s languages, songs, food, clothing, stories and customs formed part of the heritage that South Africans celebrate.
But, he said, heritage should not remain something remembered only once a year. “Our heritage is living because it resides in people. It lives in our homes and our communities.”
He pointed to grandmothers telling stories to their grandchildren, traditional healers, craftspeople, musicians and dancers as examples of people keeping SA’s heritage alive. Ramaphosa also highlighted the importance of ceremonies, faith, rituals and the languages spoken by South Africans every day.
The theme for this year’s Heritage Day is “Celebrating Our Living Heritage: Strengthening the Ties That Bind Us”.
Ramaphosa said the country has a responsibility to make sure indigenous knowledge and traditions were not lost as older generations passed away. “We must record it. We must teach it. We must practise it. And above all, we must pass it on.”
Our constitution is our heritage. It is the tie that binds us together
— President Cyril Ramaphosa
He warned that heritage could disappear if it is not passed from one generation to another, “because a heritage that is not passed from one generation to another eventually ceases to be a living heritage”.
Ramaphosa also spoke about SA’s difficult history, including dispossession, slavery, colonialism, apartheid and forced removals. “South Africans should also remember the resistance, courage and solidarity that helped bring about democracy.”
The decision by South Africans to build one country together after generations of conflict was itself part of the country’s heritage, he said. “Our constitution is our heritage. It is the tie that binds us together.”
The country’s diversity should not be viewed as something that divides the country but rather that the many cultures, languages, religions and histories make South Africa what it is, he said. Heritage should shape the country South Africans want to build — a country where people have opportunities, talent matters more than connections, public office is a responsibility and young people can dream and succeed.
South Africans should be confident about the future without forgetting where they came from, he said. “A nation cannot grow stronger unless its roots are nourished every day by its people.”
Ramaphosa called on South Africans to protect the values of unity, ubuntu and human dignity. “These three — not race, culture, language or geography — truly make us who we are.”
